shell.search.actions.account-new-user.ke.en: new user|create user|add account|new account|add operator|add admin|invite
shell.search.actions.account-new-user.ke.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the shortcut for adding a person's account. Use the words administrators would really type in the target language, including the local words for operator, administrator and invitation; keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.account-new-service.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that opens the account list ready to create a service account. A service is an organisational unit that submits data, so this is not a human sign-in; keep it clearly distinct from the shortcut for adding a person.
One-line hint under that shortcut. It names the kind of account being created: the identity a service uses to send its data in, rather than a person's login. Single line, no final period.

Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the shortcut for adding a service account. 'Onboard' is the sense of bringing a new service into the system; use whatever administrators would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.event-new.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that opens the events screen ready to record a new timeline event, such as an incident or a maintenance window. Imperative, matching the wording on the events screen.

shell.search.actions.event-new.descripti.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. 'Record' means noting something that happened so it appears on the timeline beside the reported data; the timeline is the chronological list of such events. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.event-new.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the shortcut for recording an event. The last three entries are the common kinds of event administrators look for, so use the words they would really type in the target language; keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.report-upload.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that opens the report catalogue so a report definition file can be added. 'Upload' is the act of sending that definition to the server, not printing or exporting anything. Imperative.

shell.search.actions.report-upload.descr.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. A report definition is the reusable template that gets rendered later, not a rendered document. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.report-upload.keywo.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the shortcut for adding a report definition. 'Import' here means bringing a definition file in; use the words administrators would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.explore.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that opens the analytics screen for charting and comparing reported data. It names a destination in the console, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry — users navigate by muscle memory. A verb of investigation, not of physical exploration.

shell.search.actions.explore.description.context: One-line hint under that shortcut, naming what the analytics screen offers: movement over time, side-by-side comparison, and a picture of one point in time. 'In-app' means the analysis happens in the console rather than in an exported file. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.explore.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the analytics screen. The English list deliberately holds both British and American spellings of the same verb; do the equivalent for the target language by including the spellings and synonyms users actually type, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.explore-scorecard.t.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that opens the analytics screen directly on its scorecard view. It names that view, so it must read exactly like the corresponding tab on the analytics screen. A scorecard here is a grid rating each reported value against its target band, not a sports score.

shell.search.actions.explore-scorecard.d.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. 'RAG' is the red/amber/green traffic-light rating of each value against the target ranges an administrator set for it; keep the initialism only if it is genuinely established in the target language, otherwise name the three colours. 'Cross-schema' means the board covers every schema at once instead of one at a time. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.explore-scorecard.k.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the scorecard view. The entries are the different ways people refer to traffic-light status — the initialism, the three colours spelled out, the traffic-light metaphor, and the target values being rated. Supply the equivalents users would really type in the target language, keep the widely used English forms too, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.explore-anomalies.t.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that opens the analytics screen directly on its anomalies view. It names that view, so it must read exactly like the corresponding tab on the analytics screen. An anomaly is a reported figure that looks out of line with the others, not a fault in the system.

shell.search.actions.explore-anomalies.d.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. A period is a reporting window, and the board examines each window separately to flag figures that stand out within it. 'Detection' means the system finds them automatically. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.explore-anomalies.k.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the anomalies view. The entries cover the informal ways people describe a figure that stands out, including a sudden jump. Use the words users would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.missing.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that opens the screen listing the submissions that services have not sent in yet. Keep it consistent with that screen's own heading; the sidebar uses a shortened form of the same phrase. 'Missing' describes data expected but not received, not something lost.

shell.search.actions.missing.description.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. 'Owes' is an obligation to report, not a debt of money: it is the data a service is still required to submit for the periods that have passed. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.missing.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the outstanding-submissions screen. 'Overdue' is past its deadline and 'gaps' are holes in the reported series; give the words administrators would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.dashboard.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the console's landing screen. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry — users navigate by muscle memory. Many languages keep this word untranslated; follow whatever the sidebar uses.

shell.search.actions.dashboard.descripti.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. 'Home' is the console's starting screen and 'overview' is the summary of everything at a glance. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.dashboard.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the landing screen. 'Start' is the sense of where you begin, not of starting a process. Give the words users would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.submissions.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the list of submissions, where a submission is one filled-in set of data a service has sent in for a reporting period. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry.

shell.search.actions.submissions.descrip.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. 'Browse' means looking through the list rather than searching or editing, and 'submitted data' is the figures services have already sent in. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.submissions.keyword.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the submission list. The last entry is the word used internally for the individual reported readings inside a submission; give the words users would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.schemas.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the list of schemas, i.e. the admin-defined definitions of what each service must report. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry.

shell.search.actions.schemas.description.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. 'Catalog' is simply the collection of all schema definitions held in the console; use the normal word for a catalogue in the target language and match the spelling convention used elsewhere in the console. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.schemas.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the schema list. The entries describe a schema from a user's point of view — a KPI definition, a reusable template, and the data fields it defines. Give the words administrators would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.accounts.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the account list. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry. An account is any sign-in identity, whether a person, an application or a service.

shell.search.actions.accounts.descriptio.context: One-line hint under that shortcut, listing the account roles found on that screen: a service is an organisational unit that submits data, an operator is a back-office reader, a user is an ordinary person's login and an admin holds every permission. Use exactly the role names shown on the account screens. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.accounts.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the account list. The entries are the role names plus the everyday word for the humans among them; use the role names as translated elsewhere, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.events.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the events timeline. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry. These are recorded occurrences such as incidents or maintenance, not calendar appointments.

shell.search.actions.events.description.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. 'Browse' means looking through the list, and the timeline is the chronological view of recorded occurrences that provides context for the reported figures. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.events.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the events timeline. The entries are the kinds of occurrence people look for; give the words administrators would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.reports.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the report catalogue. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry. These are report definitions that can be rendered, not rendered documents.

shell.search.actions.reports.description.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. 'Browse' is looking through the catalogue; 'render' is producing the finished document from a report definition and the data, so use a verb for generating output rather than one for drawing or translating. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.reports.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the report catalogue. The English list deliberately holds both spellings of 'catalog'; do the equivalent for the target language by covering the spellings and synonyms users type, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.audit.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the screen recording every change made in the console. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry. The sense is an inspection record, not a financial audit.

shell.search.actions.audit.description.context: One-line hint under that shortcut, naming the three things the record answers: which account acted, what they changed, and when. The English is deliberately elliptical; add the minimum verb the language needs and keep it to one short line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.audit.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the change record. 'Trail' is the sense of a documented sequence of actions that can be followed; give the words administrators would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.tools.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the maintenance screen holding the backup and restore utilities. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry.

shell.search.actions.tools.description.context: One-line hint under that shortcut. A backup is a downloadable copy of everything the console holds; restoring puts such a copy back and replaces the current contents. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.tools.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the backup and restore screen. 'Export' is taking a copy out and 'import' is bringing one back in; give the words administrators would really type in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.search.actions.settings.title.context: Row in the task-shortcut list that goes to the console's configuration screen. It names a destination, so it must read exactly like the corresponding sidebar entry.

shell.search.actions.settings.descriptio.context: One-line hint under that shortcut, naming what can be configured there. A webhook is an outbound call the console makes to another system when something happens, and normally stays in English; 'policy' here is the rule deciding whether submissions need approval before they count. Single line, no final period.

shell.search.actions.settings.keywords.context: Never displayed: extra terms the search matches against so that typing an intent finds the configuration screen. The list deliberately holds both the full word for configuration and its clipped everyday form, plus the names of the things configured there; do the same in the target language, keep the vertical bars as separators and keep everything lowercase.

shell.gridPager.rowsPerPage.context: Caption to the left of the small dropdown at the foot of a data table that chooses how many rows one page shows. Keep it short: the footer crowds this control, a count and two buttons onto a single line.

shell.gridPager.results_one.context: Stands in for the row-range summary at the foot of a data table when nothing matches the current filters. A result is one matching row. Singular form, and it is not an error message.

placeholders.count: How many rows matched; this form is used where the language's grammar calls for the singular, including zero in some languages

shell.gridPager.results_other.context: Stands in for the row-range summary at the foot of a data table when nothing matches the current filters, so in practice the count read is zero. A result is one matching row, and this is not an error message.

placeholders.count: How many rows matched, in practice 0

shell.gridPager.range.context: Tells the reader which slice of a data table's rows is currently on screen, at the foot of the table. Keep it compact — it shares one line with the page-size dropdown and the paging buttons — and keep the dash between the two row numbers.

placeholders.from: Number of the first row shown on this page, e.g. 26
placeholders.to: Number of the last row shown on this page, e.g. 50
placeholders.total: How many rows match the current filters in total, e.g. 137

shell.gridPager.previous.context: Steps a data table back one page. Imperative, about paging through rows — nothing to do with an earlier reporting period. Short: it sits beside the page counter and the forward button.

shell.gridPager.page.context: Counter between the two paging buttons at the foot of a data table. Page means one screenful of rows; keep it very compact.

placeholders.page: Number of the page currently shown, e.g. 2
placeholders.totalPages: How many pages the matching rows fill, e.g. 6

shell.gridPager.next.context: Steps a data table forward one page. Imperative, about paging through rows — not the next step of a form and not a following reporting period.

shell.rowActions.ariaLabel.context: Accessible name of the three-dot button in the last column of a table row, which opens the menu of things that can be done to that row. Describe the actions rather than the dots; never seen on screen.

shell.period.label.context: Caption above the dropdown that narrows a list to a stretch of time. Names a time range used as a filter, so a noun phrase, with no colon.

shell.period.from.context: Caption above the date-and-time box that sets where a custom range starts; the start instant itself is included. Appears only once the reader has chosen a custom range.

shell.period.to.context: Caption above the date-and-time box that sets where a custom range ends; the end instant itself is excluded. Appears only once the reader has chosen a custom range.

shell.period.interval.all.context: Choice in the time-range dropdown that imposes no date limit whatsoever, so every record is listed however old. Noun phrase naming the choice.

shell.period.interval.lastDay.context: Choice in the time-range dropdown covering the twenty-four hours immediately before now. A window that rolls with the clock — not yesterday, and not the current calendar day.

shell.period.interval.lastWeek.context: Choice in the time-range dropdown covering the seven days immediately before now, counted back from this moment rather than meaning the current or previous calendar week.

shell.period.interval.lastMonth.context: Choice in the time-range dropdown covering the thirty days immediately before now. Thirty days counted back from this moment, not the current or previous calendar month.

shell.period.interval.custom.context: Choice in the time-range dropdown that reveals two date-and-time boxes so the reader can set the start and the end themselves. Noun phrase naming a range they define.

shell.period.shift.1m.context: Choice of how far back the comparison series on the analysis screen is offset, so the same window one month earlier is drawn alongside the current one. Calendar-aware, so it lands on the same point of the previous month; a bare amount of time, with no preposition.

shell.period.shift.6m.context: Choice of how far back the comparison series on the analysis screen is offset: the same window half a year earlier. A bare amount of time, with no preposition.

shell.period.shift.1y.context: Choice of how far back the comparison series on the analysis screen is offset: the same window one year earlier, landing on the same date. A bare amount of time, with no preposition.

shell.wizard.back.context: Returns to the previous step of a multi-step dialog. Imperative, and about position in the sequence of steps rather than about browser history.

shell.wizard.finish.context: Caption of the confirming button on the last step of a multi-step dialog; pressing it carries out whatever the dialog was set up to do. Imperative, and short enough to sit beside Cancel and Back.

shell.wizard.next.context: Moves on to the following step of a multi-step dialog. Imperative and about the next step in a sequence — not a following page of rows and not a coming reporting period.

shell.drawer.collapse.context: Accessible name of the icon-only button that shrinks a widened side panel back to its normal width. The panel slides in from the edge of the screen over the page; never seen on screen.

shell.drawer.expand.context: Accessible name of the icon-only button that stretches a side panel across the whole window, which helps when editing a large schema or reading a dense submission. Never seen on screen.

shell.export.csv.context: Caption of the button above a data table that downloads every matching row as a comma-separated file. Export means writing the data out to a file the reader keeps; leave the file-format abbreviation untranslated.

shell.export.exporting.context: Replaces that caption while the rows are being fetched and the file assembled. Present progressive, and it must fit the same button as the resting caption.

shell.valueLabel.required.context: Accessible name of the red asterisk printed after the name of a value that has to be filled in before a submission can be saved. The asterisk is all the reader sees; keep this lower-case, as it reads as part of the surrounding label.

shell.valueLabel.description.context: Accessible name of the small information icon beside a value's name; hovering it reveals the explanation an administrator wrote for that value. Names the icon's purpose and is never seen on screen.

shell.valueLabel.new.context: Tiny badge marking a value that was added in the schema's current version and is being reported for the first time; it disappears once one reporting cycle has passed. One very short word: the badge sits inline after the value's name and never wraps.

shell.cadence.Daily.context: How often a value has to be reported: one figure for every day. It answers how often, so an adverb or adjective of frequency rather than a noun for the day itself, and it must fit a narrow table column, a small pill and a dropdown.

shell.cadence.Weekly.context: How often a value has to be reported: one figure for every week, weeks running Monday to Sunday. One word of frequency, in the same tight places as the other cadences.

shell.cadence.Fortnightly.context: How often a value has to be reported: one figure for every fourteen-day block, the blocks always starting on a Monday. If your language has no single word for a two-week cycle, use the shortest natural phrase.

shell.cadence.Monthly.context: How often a value has to be reported: one figure for every calendar month. One word of frequency, in a narrow column, a small pill and a dropdown.

shell.cadence.Quarterly.context: How often a value has to be reported: one figure for every three-month quarter of the year, quarters running January to March, April to June, and so on.

shell.cadence.SemiAnnually.context: How often a value has to be reported: one figure for each half of the year, January to June and July to December. Keep it as short as your language allows — the column is narrow.

shell.cadence.Yearly.context: How often a value has to be reported: one figure for every calendar year. One word of frequency, in a narrow column, a small pill and a dropdown.

shell.eventKind.PointInTime.context: Names the shape of an event's place in time: a single instant with no duration. Announced for the icon-only avatar at the start of each row of the events list and also dropped into the one-line event summary in search results, so keep it brief.

shell.eventKind.Interval.context: Names the shape of an event's place in time: a span with a known start and a known length, such as a maintenance window. Interval here means a bounded stretch of time, not a gap or a pause.

shell.eventKind.FromNowOn.context: Names the shape of an event's place in time: a span that starts at the event's own timestamp and has no known end. 'Now' is the moment the event began, not the moment the reader is looking at the screen.

shell.comments.general.context: Badge on a discussion thread attached to a schema as a whole rather than to one of its values, where the other threads show a value's name instead. Means it applies to everything, not that it is ordinary or usual. One short word that must not wrap.

shell.confirm.namedSubject.context: Pairs the kind of object about to be deleted with the object's own name, and the result is then dropped into the deletion question. Keep the name in quotation marks, using the marks conventional in your language, and put the kind of object wherever it reads naturally.

placeholders.noun: Already-translated word for the kind of object, e.g. schema, submission or account
placeholders.target: The object's own label, or its machine name when it has no label, e.g. Monthly waste KPIs

joins.into: The subject slot of the deletion question shown by the browser's confirmation prompt
joins.note: No leading or trailing space of its own; the surrounding question supplies the spacing and the question mark.

shell.confirm.cannotUndo.context: Default closing line of the browser's confirmation prompt before something is deleted, warning that there is no way back. A full sentence; some prompts replace it with a more specific consequence.

shell.confirm.delete.context: The question the browser's own confirmation prompt asks before anything is deleted: the object on the first line, the consequence after a blank line. Both line breaks are load-bearing and must survive translation. Delete is imperative, and the reader answers with the browser's own buttons, which cannot be worded here.

placeholders.subject: The kind of object plus its name, already assembled and translated, e.g. schema "Monthly waste KPIs"
placeholders.note: The consequence sentence, usually the warning that the deletion cannot be undone

shell.avatars.account.context: Accessible name of the round avatar at the start of each row in the accounts list, telling screen-reader users what kind of account it is, which role it holds, and whether it has been switched off. Never seen on screen; the middle dot separates kind from role.

placeholders.kind: Already-translated account kind, e.g. User or Application
placeholders.role: Already-translated role of the account, e.g. Operator
placeholders.context: Either empty, or the already-translated parenthesised marker for a switched-off account, e.g. " (disabled)"

shell.avatars.disabledSuffix.context: Marks an account or a schema value that an administrator has switched off, tacked onto the end of an avatar's accessible name. Disabled means deactivated on purpose, not faulty; keep the parentheses.

joins.after: The role in an account avatar's accessible name, or the data type in a schema value's
joins.note: The leading space is load-bearing and must be kept. CJK may drop it only where the following character is full-width.

shell.avatars.schema.context: Accessible name of the round avatar beside a schema's name in the schemas list, saying what the avatar stands for. Never seen on screen; a schema is an admin-defined definition of the values a service must report.

shell.avatars.schemaDisabled.context: The same accessible name when the schema has been switched off, so nothing can be submitted against it. Never seen on screen; word the parenthesised marker exactly as it is worded for switched-off accounts and values.

shell.avatars.submission.context: Accessible name of the round avatar beside a row of the submissions list when that submission has no review state worth announcing. Never seen on screen; a submission is one filled-in instance of a schema for one reporting period.

shell.avatars.submissionStatus.context: Accessible name of that same avatar when the submission does carry a state — still a draft, waiting for review, signed off, or turned down. Never seen on screen; the middle dot separates the object from its state.

placeholders.status: Already-translated state of the submission, e.g. Pending

shell.avatars.auditChange.context: Accessible name of the avatar at the start of each row in the change log, naming the kind of object that was touched and what was done to it. Never seen on screen; the middle dot separates the two.

placeholders.target: Already-translated kind of object that was affected, e.g. Schema
placeholders.change: Already-translated operation that was performed, e.g. Edit

shell.avatars.status.context: Stands in for the subject of a delivery avatar's accessible name when the screen supplies none, so the announcement still says what the state belongs to. Refers to how far a queued message has got; never seen on screen.

shell.avatars.deliveryStatus.context: Accessible name of the avatar beside a queued email or webhook delivery, naming what is being delivered and how far it has got. Never seen on screen; the middle dot separates the two.

placeholders.label: What the delivery concerns — usually the recipient address or the webhook event name, e.g. ops@contoso.com

shell.avatars.schemaValue.context: Accessible name of the small avatar beside a single value inside a schema, naming the value's data type and, where it applies, that the value has been switched off. Never seen on screen.

placeholders.type: Already-translated data type of the value, e.g. Integer
placeholders.context: Either empty, or the already-translated parenthesised marker for a switched-off value, e.g. " (disabled)"

shell.submissionStatus.Draft.context: State of a submission that has been started and saved but not yet handed in, so nothing is counted or reviewed yet. A lifecycle of its own, independent of review; announced as part of an avatar's accessible name and never shown on screen.

shell.submissionStatus.Pending.context: State of a submission that has been handed in and is waiting for a reviewer's decision; its figures are held out of the live data until then. Means awaiting a decision, not unfinished.

shell.submissionStatus.Approved.context: State of a submission that every required reviewer has signed off, so its figures now count as live. Use the same wording as elsewhere for approving a submission.

shell.submissionStatus.Rejected.context: State of a submission a reviewer turned down: its figures are left out of the live data, though the submission stays visible so the service can see what happened.

shell.submissionStatus.NotRequired.context: State of a submission that needs no review at all, because no approval policy covers it, so it counts as live as soon as it is accepted. Says that approval is not required — never that the submission itself is unnecessary.

shell.deliveryStatus.Pending.context: State of a queued email or webhook that is waiting for the sender to pick it up; no attempt has been made yet. Announced as part of an avatar's accessible name and never shown on screen.

shell.deliveryStatus.Sending.context: State of a queued email or webhook that the sender has taken up and is delivering at this moment. Names an attempt in progress rather than a finished one.

shell.deliveryStatus.Sent.context: State of a queued email or webhook the mail or web server accepted, so delivery is done as far as this product can tell. Announced as part of an avatar's accessible name and never shown on screen.

shell.deliveryStatus.Failed.context: State of a queued email or webhook that will not be attempted again, either because the retries ran out or because the problem cannot be recovered from. A final state, not a temporary hitch.

shell.auditChange.Create.context: Operation recorded in the change log when an object was newly added. Announced as part of the accessible name of the avatar starting each log row, so it is never read as an abbreviation and never shown on screen; a bare verbal noun or infinitive naming the operation, not an instruction.

shell.auditChange.Edit.context: Operation recorded in the change log when an existing object was modified. Names the operation that was performed, not an instruction to edit anything.

shell.auditChange.Delete.context: Operation recorded in the change log when an object was removed — or, for access credentials, which are never really removed, when it was revoked. Names the operation that was performed.

shell.auditChange.Approve.context: Operation recorded in the change log when a reviewer signed off a submission, kept separate from ordinary edits so decisions can be filtered out. Use the same wording as elsewhere for approving a submission.

shell.auditChange.Reject.context: Operation recorded in the change log when a reviewer turned a submission down; the reason, when one was given, is stored alongside it. Names the decision that was taken.

shell.auditTarget.User.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: an account belonging to a person, which can sign in to the console. Announced as part of the avatar's accessible name in the change log and never shown on screen; keep it consistent with the account kind of the same name.

shell.auditTarget.Account.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: an account used by a program rather than a person, able to call the API only. The two account entries are told apart by the kind the account had when it was changed.

shell.auditTarget.Schema.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: a schema, the admin-defined definition of which values a service must report and how often. Use the same word for it as everywhere else.

shell.auditTarget.ApiKey.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: an access credential issued to an account. Key means a credential, never a keyboard key; keep the abbreviation for the programming interface untranslated.

shell.auditTarget.Submission.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: one filled-in instance of a schema for one reporting period. Singular noun, matching the wording used for submissions elsewhere.

shell.auditTarget.Report.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: a saved report, meaning a stored selection of values and periods that can be rendered or exported. Not a report in the sense of an incident report.

shell.auditTarget.SchemaHistory.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: one saved snapshot of an earlier version of a schema. Deliberately distinct from the live schema, so removing a snapshot is not mistaken for deleting the schema itself.

shell.auditTarget.ApprovalRule.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: a rule saying whether submissions for a given service or schema need signing off, and by whom. Rule in the sense of a configured policy.

shell.auditTarget.Settings.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: any of the configuration areas saved from the settings screens, such as mail, notifications or the default approval policy. Recorded generically so the log answers who changed configuration and when.

shell.auditTarget.Backup.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: the restoring of a backup, either of the collected data or of the configuration. Names the backup itself; the operation is recorded separately.

shell.auditTarget.Event.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: an occurrence an administrator recorded on the timeline, such as a maintenance window or an incident. Not a system or log event.

shell.auditTarget.CommentThread.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: a whole discussion attached to a schema or to one of its values, covering it being opened, marked settled, reopened or removed. A thread is a series of replies about one topic.

shell.auditTarget.Comment.context: Kind of object a change-log entry refers to: a single message within such a discussion, as opposed to the discussion as a whole. Singular noun.

shell.auditTargetInitials.User.context: Abbreviation of the kind of object a change-log entry refers to, rendered inside a small circular avatar at the start of the row; here, an account belonging to a person. Two characters at most in every language, and a single character where the script has no natural two-character abbreviation.

shell.auditTargetInitials.Account.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row for an account used by a program rather than a person. Two characters at most, one where the script has no natural two-character form, and it must differ from the abbreviation for a person's account.

shell.auditTargetInitials.Schema.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about a schema. Two characters at most, and it must not collide with the abbreviation used for a schema's saved version history.

shell.auditTargetInitials.ApiKey.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about an access credential. Two characters at most; abbreviate the words your own language uses for a credential rather than transliterating the English.

shell.auditTargetInitials.Submission.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about a submission. Two characters at most, and it must stay distinct from the abbreviations for schemas and settings.

shell.auditTargetInitials.Report.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about a saved report. Two characters at most, one where the script has no natural two-character form.

shell.auditTargetInitials.SchemaHistory.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about a saved snapshot of an earlier schema version. Two characters at most, and distinguishable from the abbreviation for the schema itself.

shell.auditTargetInitials.ApprovalRule.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about a rule governing which submissions need signing off. Two characters at most, one where the script has no natural two-character form.

shell.auditTargetInitials.Settings.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about a saved configuration area. Two characters at most, one where the script has no natural two-character form.

shell.auditTargetInitials.Backup.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about a backup being restored. Two characters at most, one where the script has no natural two-character form.

shell.auditTargetInitials.Event.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about an administrator-recorded timeline occurrence. Two characters at most, one where the script has no natural two-character form.

shell.auditTargetInitials.CommentThread.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about a whole discussion. Two characters at most, and it must stay distinct from the abbreviation for a single message.

shell.auditTargetInitials.Comment.context: Abbreviation shown inside the small circular avatar of a change-log row about one message inside a discussion. Two characters at most, and distinguishable from the abbreviation for the discussion as a whole.

shell.valueType.String.context: Data type of a value inside a schema: free-form text, optionally constrained by a length or a pattern. Announced as part of the accessible name of the avatar beside the value and never shown on screen, so name the type as programmers in your language would, spelled out rather than abbreviated.

shell.valueType.Integer.context: Data type of a value inside a schema: a whole number, optionally bounded by a minimum and a maximum. Spoken by screen readers only, so spell the type name out.

shell.valueType.Number.context: Data type of a value inside a schema: a number that may have a fractional part, as opposed to the whole-number type. Choose wording that clearly contrasts with the whole-number type rather than a generic word for number.

shell.valueType.Date.context: Data type of a value inside a schema: a date, optionally carrying a time of day as well. Spoken by screen readers only, so spell the type name out.

shell.valueType.Boolean.context: Data type of a value inside a schema: a yes-or-no flag with only two possible states. Use the term programmers in your language use for this type; many languages keep the English word.

shell.valueTypeInitials.String.context: Single-character abbreviation of a value's data type, rendered inside the small circular avatar beside the value in a schema; here, the free-form text type. One character is strongly preferred and two is the hard maximum, and each type's abbreviation has to differ from all the others.

shell.valueTypeInitials.Integer.context: Single-character abbreviation shown in the small circular avatar for a whole-number value. One character preferred, two at the very most, and it must differ from the abbreviation chosen for the fractional-number type.

shell.valueTypeInitials.Number.context: Single-character abbreviation shown in the small circular avatar for a value that may have a fractional part. One character preferred, two at the very most, and it must not collide with the whole-number abbreviation.

shell.valueTypeInitials.Date.context: Single-character abbreviation shown in the small circular avatar for a date value. One character preferred, two at the very most.

shell.valueTypeInitials.Boolean.context: Single-character abbreviation shown in the small circular avatar for a yes-or-no value. One character preferred, two at the very most.

shell.capabilities.groups.schemas.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the rights over schemas — the admin-defined definitions of what a service must report. Noun phrase, no period, and short: the groups sit stacked in a narrow panel.

shell.capabilities.groups.submissions.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the rights over submissions — the filled-in sets of data services send in for a reporting period. Noun phrase, no period.

shell.capabilities.groups.analytics.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the rights to read and analyse reported data rather than change it. Noun phrase, no period.

shell.capabilities.groups.reports.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the rights over report definitions and their rendered output. Noun phrase, no period.

shell.capabilities.groups.accountsKeys.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, covering both accounts and the API keys attached to them. A key here is a credential an application uses to authenticate, never a keyboard key or a database key. Keep the two nouns joined as the language normally joins them; no period.

shell.capabilities.groups.oversight.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the supervisory and compliance rights: the change record, personal-data handling and whole-system backups. Choose a word for supervision or governance rather than one for surveillance. Noun phrase, no period.

shell.capabilities.groups.notificationsI.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the rights over outbound messaging: email and notifications, webhooks, and connections to other systems. Keep the two nouns joined as the language normally joins them; no period.

shell.capabilities.groups.settings.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the rights over the console's global configuration. Use the same word as the sidebar entry of the same name; no period.

shell.capabilities.groups.events.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the rights over timeline events such as incidents and maintenance. Noun phrase, no period.

shell.capabilities.groups.comments.context: Small heading above one block of permission checkboxes in the account permissions panel, grouping the rights over discussion threads attached to schemas. Noun phrase, no period.

shell.capabilities.items.schemasRead.lab.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to schemas. It names a right the account will hold, so use the form your language uses in a list of permissions — an infinitive or a noun phrase — rather than an imperative telling the reader to do it. Keep it short: the checkboxes sit two to a row.

shell.capabilities.items.schemasRead.des.en: Browse the schema catalog, detail and history.
shell.capabilities.items.schemasRead.des.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: open the list of schemas, look at an individual schema and inspect its earlier versions. It is read-only — no creating or editing — and it is what makes the schema screens reachable at all.

shell.capabilities.items.schemasManage.l.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants full control over schemas. 'Manage' means being allowed to change them, in contrast to the view-only right listed beside it; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.

shell.capabilities.items.schemasManage.d.en: Create, edit, clone and delete schemas.
shell.capabilities.items.schemasManage.d.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do to schema definitions: add new ones, change them, copy an existing one as the starting point for another, and remove them. It does not include the right to view schemas — that box must be ticked as well for the screens to be reachable.

shell.capabilities.items.submissionsRead.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to submissions, the filled-in sets of data services send in. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.
Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: look at submitted data for every service, not only its own. Read-only, and it is the right that makes the submission screens reachable.

shell.capabilities.items.submissionsSubm.context: Caption of the checkbox that lets the account enter data in a service's place — for instance an administrator keying in figures a service has not entered itself. 'On behalf' means acting for someone else, and the object left unsaid is the service; add it if the language needs it. Keep it short.

shell.capabilities.items.submissionsSubm.en: Create, edit and bulk-import submissions for a service.
shell.capabilities.items.submissionsSubm.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do for a service: enter a new submission, correct an existing one, and load many at once from a file. It covers entering and changing data, not removing or approving it, and it does not include the right to view submissions.

shell.capabilities.items.submissionsDele.context: Caption of the checkbox that lets the account remove submissions outright. Deliberately separate from the right to enter and edit them, because the effect cannot be undone; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: erase a submission for good, with no way to recover it afterwards. Keep that finality plain — it is the reason this right is granted separately from editing.

shell.capabilities.items.submissionsAppr.context: Caption of the checkbox that lets the account sign off submissions that are waiting for a decision. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, and keep the verb consistent with the approve action on the submission screens.

Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: decide on submissions that are waiting for sign-off, accepting them or sending them back. 'Pending' means awaiting that decision, not merely recent. The account also needs the right to view submissions in order to reach the queue.

shell.capabilities.items.queryRead.label.context: Caption of the checkbox that lets the account run its own queries against the collected data from outside the console, typically from a spreadsheet or a reporting tool. 'Query' is the sense of interrogating stored data; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.queryRead.descr.en: Use the OData feed and ad-hoc query endpoint.
shell.capabilities.items.queryRead.descr.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: read the collected data through the machine interfaces — the standing OData feed that external tools connect to, and the endpoint that answers one-off queries. Leave 'OData' in English, as it is the name of a protocol; 'ad-hoc' means a query composed on the spot rather than a saved one.

shell.capabilities.items.exploreRead.lab.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants access to the analytics screen. It names the same feature as the sidebar entry, so use that wording; a verb of investigation, not of physical exploration.

shell.capabilities.items.exploreRead.des.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: use the analytics built into the console — charts, comparisons, the scorecard and the anomaly board. 'In-app' contrasts with reading the data through an external tool, which is a separate right.

shell.capabilities.items.statusRead.labe.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants access to the reporting-progress views. 'Status' here is how completely services have reported, not the health of the system; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.statusRead.desc.en: See cross-service status and missing-submission analytics.
shell.capabilities.items.statusRead.desc.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account see: how far every service has got with its reporting, and which submissions are still outstanding for periods that have passed. Read-only.

shell.capabilities.items.reportsRead.lab.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to reports. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.

shell.capabilities.items.reportsRead.des.en: Browse and render the report catalog.
shell.capabilities.items.reportsRead.des.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: look through the collection of report definitions and produce their output from the data. 'Render' is generating the finished document, so use a verb for producing output rather than one for drawing or translating.

shell.capabilities.items.reportsManage.l.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants control over report definitions, in contrast to the view-and-render right listed beside it. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.reportsManage.d.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: add report definitions by sending the definition file to the server, and remove them again. It concerns the definitions, not the documents they produce, and it does not include the right to view or render them.

shell.capabilities.items.accountsRead.la.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to accounts — the sign-in identities of people, applications and services. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.accountsRead.de.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: look through the list of accounts and their details. Read-only, and it is the right that makes the account screens reachable.

shell.capabilities.items.accountsManage..context: Caption of the checkbox that grants control over accounts, in contrast to the view-only right listed beside it. This is the most powerful right in the panel, since it includes handing out permissions; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.accountsManage..en: Create, edit and delete accounts and their permissions.
shell.capabilities.items.accountsManage..context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: add accounts, change or remove them, and decide which permissions each one holds — including granting rights it holds itself. 'Permissions' means exactly the checkboxes in this panel.

shell.capabilities.items.apiKeysRead.lab.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to API keys. A key here is a credential an application sends to prove who it is, never a keyboard key; leave 'API' in English. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.apiKeysRead.des.en: See the API keys attached to accounts.
shell.capabilities.items.apiKeysRead.des.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account see: which credentials exist against each account, when they expire and what they are for. It does not reveal the secret value itself, and it does not allow creating or withdrawing keys.

shell.capabilities.items.apiKeysManage.l.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants control over API keys, in contrast to the view-only right listed beside it. Leave 'API' in English; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.apiKeysManage.d.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: create new credentials for an account and withdraw existing ones so they stop working immediately. 'Issue' is handing a credential out and 'revoke' is cancelling it — use the established security terms in the target language, and keep them consistent with the API key screens.

shell.capabilities.items.auditRead.label.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants access to the record of everything that has been changed in the console. The sense is an inspection record, not a financial audit; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.

shell.capabilities.items.auditRead.descr.en: Read and export the audit trail.
shell.capabilities.items.auditRead.descr.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: read the chronological record of who changed what and when, and download it as a file. The record can only ever be read, never altered, so keep any verb clearly read-only.

shell.capabilities.items.privacyRead.lab.context: Caption of the checkbox that lets the account extract everything the system holds about one individual, as data-protection law requires on request. 'Personal data' is the established legal term, so use the wording your jurisdiction uses; the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.

shell.capabilities.items.privacyRead.des.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: produce, for one named person, a downloadable file of all the data held about them, in answer to a subject access request. 'Data subject' is the person the data is about — use the standard data-protection term. It grants no right to delete anything.

shell.capabilities.items.privacyManage.l.context: Caption of the checkbox covering the two destructive data-protection operations: wiping one person's data and applying the storage time limits. The slash joins two separate things, so keep a compact form that fits a narrow checkbox row; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.privacyManage.d.en: Erase personal data and run retention.
shell.capabilities.items.privacyManage.d.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: permanently remove the data held about a person, and start the purge that deletes records older than the configured limits — which normally runs on its own schedule. Both are irreversible, so keep the verbs unambiguous; 'retention' is the policy governing how long data is kept, not the act of keeping it.

shell.capabilities.items.backupRead.labe.context: Caption of the checkbox that lets the account take away a copy of everything the console holds. 'Export' is producing that copy as a file to download; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.

shell.capabilities.items.backupRead.desc.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: download the complete contents of the console as a single file. 'Full' means nothing is left out, which is also why the right is worth granting sparingly; it does not allow putting a copy back.

shell.capabilities.items.backupManage.la.context: Caption of the checkbox that lets the account load a previously taken copy back in. Keep it clearly distinct from the neighbouring right that only downloads a copy; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.backupManage.de.en: Restore the registry from a backup.
shell.capabilities.items.backupManage.de.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: rebuild the console's entire contents from a backup file, which replaces everything currently stored. Say plainly that existing data is overwritten; this is the most destructive right in the panel.

shell.capabilities.items.notificationsRe.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to the messaging setup: how mail is sent, what the messages say, and which ones have gone out. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.

shell.capabilities.items.notificationsRe.en: See email/notification config, templates and the outbox.
shell.capabilities.items.notificationsRe.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account see: the mail and notification settings, the editable message templates, and the queue of messages waiting to be sent or already sent. Keep 'template' as the reusable text with placeholders, and use the same word for the outgoing queue as the mail screens use. Read-only.

shell.capabilities.items.notificationsMa.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants control over the messaging setup, in contrast to the view-only right listed beside it. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.notificationsMa.en: Edit email/notification config and templates; send mail.
shell.capabilities.items.notificationsMa.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: change the mail and notification settings and the message templates, and actually send mail — including a test message and pushing the waiting queue out now. It does not include the right to view that configuration.

shell.capabilities.items.webhooksRead.la.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to webhooks. A webhook is a call the console makes out to another system when something happens; the term normally stays in English. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.webhooksRead.de.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account see: the addresses the console calls out to, and the log of each attempted call with whether it succeeded. A 'delivery' is one such attempt. Read-only.

shell.capabilities.items.webhooksManage..context: Caption of the checkbox that grants control over webhooks, in contrast to the view-only right listed beside it. Leave 'webhook' in English if that is what the rest of the console does; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.webhooksManage..en: Create/edit webhooks, rotate secrets, redeliver and drain.
shell.capabilities.items.webhooksManage..context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: add and change the addresses called out to, replace the shared secret used to sign each call, send a failed call again, and push the waiting queue out immediately. 'Rotate' means replacing a secret with a fresh one; 'redeliver' means retrying a specific failed call; 'drain' means emptying the queue by sending what is in it now.

shell.capabilities.items.integrationsRea.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to integrations — configured connections to other products. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.

shell.capabilities.items.integrationsRea.en: See integrations (e.g. Microsoft Teams) and their connection.
shell.capabilities.items.integrationsRea.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account see: which external products the console is wired up to and how that connection is configured. 'Microsoft Teams' is a product name and must be left exactly as it is; 'e.g.' introduces it as the example currently supported. Read-only.

shell.capabilities.items.integrationsMan.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants control over integrations, in contrast to the view-only right listed beside it. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.integrationsMan.en: Create/edit integrations, edit the connection, run/test and drain.
shell.capabilities.items.integrationsMan.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: add and change connections to other products, edit the credentials of the connection itself, trigger a run or a test message on demand, and push the waiting queue of outgoing messages out now. 'Run' here is a verb — executing a pass immediately rather than waiting for the schedule.

shell.capabilities.items.settingsRead.la.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to the console's global configuration. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, and the same word for settings as the sidebar entry.

shell.capabilities.items.settingsRead.de.en: Read global settings (e.g. the default approval policy).
shell.capabilities.items.settingsRead.de.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account see: the settings that apply across the whole console, the example given being the rule that decides whether submissions must be approved before they count. 'Global' means system-wide rather than per service or per schema. Read-only.

shell.capabilities.items.settingsManage..context: Caption of the checkbox that allows changing the console's global configuration, in contrast to the view-only right listed beside it. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.settingsManage..en: Change global settings (e.g. the default approval policy).
shell.capabilities.items.settingsManage..context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: alter the settings that apply across the whole console, such as the default rule deciding whether submissions need approval. Keep the verb clearly one of modification, and mirror the wording of the neighbouring read-only right so the pair reads as a contrast.

shell.capabilities.items.eventsRead.labe.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to the events timeline. Events are recorded occurrences such as incidents or maintenance, not calendar appointments; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.eventsRead.desc.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: look through the chronological list of recorded occurrences that gives context to the reported figures. Read-only, and it is the right that makes the events screen reachable.

shell.capabilities.items.eventsManage.la.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants control over events, in contrast to the view-only right listed beside it. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.eventsManage.de.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do to timeline events: record new ones, correct them and remove them. It does not include the right to view the timeline, which has to be ticked as well.

shell.capabilities.items.commentsRead.la.context: Caption of the checkbox that grants read access to the discussions attached to schemas. Without it the account sees no comments at all, so this is the base right of the three in this group; use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights.

shell.capabilities.items.commentsRead.de.en: See comment threads on schemas (and their values).
shell.capabilities.items.commentsRead.de.context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account see: the discussion threads attached to a schema as a whole and to the individual values it defines. A thread is one conversation with its replies. Read-only, and required before either of the other two comment rights has any effect.

shell.capabilities.items.commentsCreate..context: Caption of the checkbox that lets the account take part in discussions, as opposed to only reading them or moderating everyone's. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, not an imperative.

shell.capabilities.items.commentsCreate..en: Start new threads and reply to existing ones; edit your own comments.
shell.capabilities.items.commentsCreate..context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do: open a new discussion thread, add replies to threads that are still open, and change the wording of comments it wrote itself. 'Your own' is the limit that matters here — someone else's comments stay untouchable. It also needs the right to view comments.

shell.capabilities.items.commentsManage..context: Caption of the checkbox that grants moderation of every discussion, not merely participation. Use the permission form your language uses in a list of rights, and keep it distinct from the two comment rights listed beside it.

shell.capabilities.items.commentsManage..en: Edit, delete or resolve/reopen any comment or thread — not just your own.
shell.capabilities.items.commentsManage..context: Explains what ticking that box lets the account do to anyone's comments and threads: reword them, remove them, and close a thread as settled or open it again. Closing a thread locks it against new replies until it is reopened. The dash introduces the contrast with the participation right, whose holder may only touch its own comments — keep that contrast explicit.

shell.expression.empty.context: Reported under the formula box of a calculated schema value when the box is blank but a formula is required. It is a complaint about missing input, not a neutral 'nothing here' notice, so keep it as an error; 'expression' is the product's term for the formula written in its own small language.

shell.expression.invalid.context: Last-resort message under the formula box when the parser rejects the formula but gives no reason of its own — normally a specific message replaces it. It underlines the wrongly written part of the formula in the editor, so keep it short and general; 'invalid' means it cannot be parsed, not that the result is wrong.

shell.expression.editorAriaLabel.context: Announced by a screen reader for the multi-line code box where a formula is typed, which has no visible label of its own. Name the control, and write it out in full — never abbreviate it — using the same word for 'expression' as the rest of the console.

shell.expression.lint.unknownFunction.context: Hover message on the red underline drawn under a function call in the formula when the evaluator has no function by that name — usually a typing mistake. Keep the straight single quotes: they delimit the exact text found in the formula, which must be reproduced as typed and never translated or corrected. 'Function' means one of the built-in operations of the formula language.

placeholders.name: The name exactly as it appears in the formula, spelling mistakes included, e.g. summ

shell.expression.lint.unknownValue.context: Hover message on the red underline drawn under a name in the formula that is neither a function nor one of the values available to it. Here 'value' means a data field defined by the schema and referred to by name in the formula — not an amount or a quantity, and the same word the schema screens use for those fields. Keep the straight single quotes and reproduce the name exactly as typed.

placeholders.name: The name exactly as it appears in the formula, spelling mistakes included, e.g. revenu

shell.expression.runtime.averageArgument.en: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got {{type}}.
shell.expression.runtime.averageArgument.context: Reported when the formula is worked out and average() is handed something it cannot average — text, a date or an object. Leave 'average()' exactly as it is, parentheses included: it is the function name in the formula language. The wording is deliberately technical and impersonal, so keep it as a statement about the call rather than rewriting it as advice to the reader; 'numeric or boolean' names the two kinds of value it does accept.

placeholders.type: English lower-case name of the offending argument's data type, taken from a fixed list, e.g. string

shell.expression.runtime.higherThanArity.context: Reported when the formula is worked out and higher_than() has been given too few arguments. Everything inside and including the parentheses is formula-language syntax and stays exactly as written — the function name with its underscore, and the three argument names in that order. Only any surrounding wording is translated.

shell.expression.runtime.higherThanNumer.context: Reported when the formula is worked out and higher_than() has been given arguments of the right number but the wrong kind, so they cannot be read as figures. Leave 'higher_than()' exactly as it is, underscore and parentheses included. Keep it distinct from the message about the wrong number of arguments, which is shown in the same place.

shell.expression.runtime.types.undefined.context: Dropped into the average() error message to name the data type of the offending argument. It is the formula language's own name for 'no value was supplied at all', and it must be left in English exactly as written — an administrator matches it against the language documentation. Lower case, no punctuation, no surrounding spaces.

joins.after: The average() argument message, in place of the data-type placeholder at the end of the sentence
joins.example: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got undefined.
joins.note: It lands mid-sentence just before the final full stop, so add no capital letter, no article and no space of your own.

shell.expression.runtime.types.object.context: Dropped into the average() error message to name the data type of the offending argument. It is the formula language's own name for a structured value rather than a single figure, and it must be left in English exactly as written. Lower case, no punctuation, no surrounding spaces.

joins.after: The average() argument message, in place of the data-type placeholder at the end of the sentence
joins.example: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got object.
joins.note: It lands mid-sentence just before the final full stop, so add no capital letter, no article and no space of your own.

shell.expression.runtime.types.boolean.context: Dropped into the average() error message to name the data type of the offending argument. It is the formula language's own name for a true/false value and must be left in English exactly as written, even though the sentence around it is translated. Lower case, no punctuation, no surrounding spaces.

joins.after: The average() argument message, in place of the data-type placeholder at the end of the sentence
joins.example: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got boolean.
joins.note: It lands mid-sentence just before the final full stop, so add no capital letter, no article and no space of your own.

shell.expression.runtime.types.number.context: Dropped into the average() error message to name the data type of the offending argument. It is the formula language's own name for a numeric value and must be left in English exactly as written; here it appears because the figure was one the language cannot work with, such as infinity. Lower case, no punctuation, no surrounding spaces.

joins.after: The average() argument message, in place of the data-type placeholder at the end of the sentence
joins.example: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got number.
joins.note: It lands mid-sentence just before the final full stop, so add no capital letter, no article and no space of your own.

shell.expression.runtime.types.bigint.context: Dropped into the average() error message to name the data type of the offending argument. It is the formula language's own name for a whole number of unlimited size, written as one word, and it must be left in English exactly as written. Lower case, no punctuation, no surrounding spaces.

joins.after: The average() argument message, in place of the data-type placeholder at the end of the sentence
joins.example: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got bigint.
joins.note: It lands mid-sentence just before the final full stop, so add no capital letter, no article and no space of your own.

shell.expression.runtime.types.string.context: Dropped into the average() error message to name the data type of the offending argument. It is the formula language's own name for a piece of text and must be left in English exactly as written, not replaced by the everyday word for text in the target language. Lower case, no punctuation, no surrounding spaces.

joins.after: The average() argument message, in place of the data-type placeholder at the end of the sentence
joins.example: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got string.
joins.note: It lands mid-sentence just before the final full stop, so add no capital letter, no article and no space of your own.

shell.expression.runtime.types.symbol.context: Dropped into the average() error message to name the data type of the offending argument. It is the formula language's own name for a unique internal marker — never something a person would type into a formula — and it must be left in English exactly as written. Lower case, no punctuation, no surrounding spaces.

joins.after: The average() argument message, in place of the data-type placeholder at the end of the sentence
joins.example: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got symbol.
joins.note: It lands mid-sentence just before the final full stop, so add no capital letter, no article and no space of your own.

shell.expression.runtime.types.function.context: Dropped into the average() error message to name the data type of the offending argument. It is the formula language's own name for an operation rather than a value — typically the result of naming a built-in without calling it — and it must be left in English exactly as written. Lower case, no punctuation, no surrounding spaces.

joins.after: The average() argument message, in place of the data-type placeholder at the end of the sentence
joins.example: average() expects numeric or boolean arguments, got function.
joins.note: It lands mid-sentence just before the final full stop, so add no capital letter, no article and no space of your own.

shell.expression.keywords.true.context: Grey explanatory note beside the suggestion 'true' in the formula editor's completion list. The suggested word itself is typed into the formula in English and is never translated; this note only says what kind of thing it is — a fixed truth value written straight into the formula. Lower case, no final period, and very short: it shares one line with the word it explains.

shell.expression.keywords.false.context: Grey explanatory note beside the suggestion 'false' in the formula editor's completion list. The suggested word is typed into the formula in English and is never translated; this note only classifies it as a fixed truth value written straight into the formula. Use exactly the same wording as the note for 'true', since both are the same kind of thing. Lower case, no final period.

shell.expression.keywords.null.context: Grey explanatory note beside the suggestion 'null' in the formula editor's completion list. The word 'null' is typed into the formula in English and is never translated; it stands for the complete absence of a value, which is different from zero or from empty text. Keep 'literal' as the term for a value written directly into the formula. Lower case, no final period.

shell.expression.keywords.and.context: Grey explanatory note beside the suggestion 'and' in the formula editor's completion list. It classifies the operator: the whole condition holds only when both sides hold. The operator itself is typed in English and never translated, and the note must stay clearly different from the ones for 'or' and 'not'. Lower case, no final period.

shell.expression.keywords.or.context: Grey explanatory note beside the suggestion 'or' in the formula editor's completion list. It classifies the operator: the condition holds when at least one side holds, including when both do — the inclusive sense, never 'one or the other but not both'. The operator itself is typed in English and never translated. Lower case, no final period.

shell.expression.keywords.not.context: Grey explanatory note beside the suggestion 'not' in the formula editor's completion list. It classifies the operator: it reverses the single condition that follows it, unlike 'and' and 'or', which join two. The operator itself is typed in English and never translated. Lower case, no final period.

shell.expression.keywords.in.context: Grey explanatory note beside the suggestion 'in' in the formula editor's completion list. It classifies the operator: it checks whether the value on the left is one of the listed values on the right — an equality test against a set, not the everyday preposition and not a range check. The operator itself is typed in English and never translated. Lower case, no final period.

shell.expression.keywords.like.context: Grey explanatory note beside the suggestion 'like' in the formula editor's completion list. It classifies the operator: it compares text against a pattern in which % stands for any run of characters and _ for exactly one, rather than testing for equality or resemblance. Keep 'SQL' in English as the name of the query language whose convention this follows, and keep 'match' in the sense of matching a pattern. Lower case, no final period.

shell.expression.functions.if.descriptio.en: Returns "then" when the condition is true, otherwise "else".
shell.expression.functions.if.descriptio.context: Description shown in the small panel beside the highlighted entry in the formula editor's suggestion list, where an administrator is writing the formula of a calculated schema value. Keep the two quoted words in English: they name the second and third arguments as they appear in the untranslated call signature shown next to this text, so the sentence says the function gives back the second argument when the condition holds and the third when it does not. One line, ending with a period.

shell.expression.functions.average.descr.en: Mean of the numeric arguments. Booleans count as 1/0; nulls are ignored.
