shell.expression.functions.average.descr.context: Suggestion-panel description for the average function in the formula editor. 'Mean' is the arithmetic average — the total divided by how many were counted. Explain that a true/false argument is counted as the figures 1 and 0, and that arguments with no value at all are left out of both the total and the count. Leave the function name, which is shown untranslated beside this text, in English; keep the digits as digits.

shell.expression.functions.higher_than.d.en: True when value exceeds reference by more than percentage% (e.g. 50 = 50%).
shell.expression.functions.higher_than.d.context: Suggestion-panel description for the higher_than function in the formula editor. The name keeps its underscore and is never translated. It holds true only when the first figure is more than the given percentage above the second, and the percentage is written as a whole number, which is what the example in brackets shows; 'reference' is the figure being compared against, and 'exceeds' means strictly greater, not equal.

shell.expression.functions.coalesce.desc.en: First argument that is not null.
shell.expression.functions.coalesce.desc.context: Suggestion-panel description for the coalesce function in the formula editor, whose name stays in English. It works through the arguments from left to right and gives back the first one that has a value, which is how a fallback default is written. 'Null' is the formula language's word for the complete absence of a value, distinct from zero or empty text.

shell.expression.functions.isNull.descri.en: True when the value is null.
shell.expression.functions.isNull.descri.context: Suggestion-panel description for the isNull function in the formula editor; the name keeps its English spelling and its capital letter in the middle. It yields true when the argument has no value at all — which is not the same as zero, false or empty text.

shell.expression.functions.len.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the len function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated name stays in English. 'Length' means how many characters the text contains, not how many words and not a physical measurement.

shell.expression.functions.now.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the now function in the formula editor. 'Current' means the present moment, and the moment is given in UTC — not in the reader's own time zone, which matters when a formula compares it with a submitted date. Leave 'UTC' as it is.

shell.expression.functions.today.descrip.context: Suggestion-panel description for the today function in the formula editor. It gives today's date in UTC with the time part set to the start of the day, which is what makes it comparable with dates that carry no time. Leave 'UTC' as it is, and keep it clearly distinct from the function that returns the current moment.

shell.expression.functions.year.descript.context: Suggestion-panel description for the year function in the formula editor. 'Component' means one part pulled out of a date — here the year as a number. Keep the same word for 'component' across all the date-part functions in this list.

shell.expression.functions.month.descrip.context: Suggestion-panel description for the month function in the formula editor. It pulls the month out of a date as a number, and the bracketed range says that counting starts at one for January. Keep the numerals and the range exactly as written.

shell.expression.functions.dayOfMonth.de.context: Suggestion-panel description for the dayOfMonth function in the formula editor, whose English name stays as it is. It gives the day number within the month, as shown by the bracketed range; keep it clearly distinct from the day-of-week and day-of-year functions listed beside it.

shell.expression.functions.dayOfWeek.des.context: Suggestion-panel description for the dayOfWeek function in the formula editor. The important point is the numbering: it starts at zero with Sunday, whatever day the week conventionally starts on in the target locale, so keep 'Sunday' and the zero exactly as they are rather than adapting them.

shell.expression.functions.dayOfYear.des.context: Suggestion-panel description for the dayOfYear function in the formula editor. It counts the days from the start of the year, and the bracketed range shows that a leap year reaches 366. Keep the numerals as written and keep it distinct from the day-of-month function.

shell.expression.functions.weekOfYear.de.context: Suggestion-panel description for the weekOfYear function in the formula editor. Leave 'ISO-8601' exactly as written: it is the name of the international standard that fixes which week counts as the first one, and it is the reason the result can differ from a local way of counting weeks.

shell.expression.functions.hour.descript.context: Suggestion-panel description for the hour function in the formula editor. The bracketed range says the hour is on the 24-hour clock, so no morning/afternoon marker is involved. Keep the numerals as written and use the same word for 'component' as the other date-part functions.

shell.expression.functions.minute.descri.context: Suggestion-panel description for the minute function in the formula editor. It pulls the minutes out of a date and time, within the range shown in brackets. Keep the numerals as written and match the wording of the neighbouring hour and second functions.

shell.expression.functions.second.descri.context: Suggestion-panel description for the second function in the formula editor. Here 'second' is the unit of time, never the ordinal 'the second one'; it pulls the seconds out of a date and time, within the range shown in brackets.

shell.expression.functions.abs.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the abs function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. It gives the size of a number with the sign discarded, so a negative figure comes back positive. Use the established mathematical term in the target language.

shell.expression.functions.ceiling.descr.en: Smallest integer greater than or equal to the number.
shell.expression.functions.ceiling.descr.context: Suggestion-panel description for the ceiling function in the formula editor. It rounds upwards, to the nearest whole number that is not below the figure given — so it must read clearly differently from the floor function directly beside it in the list. Use the established mathematical term rather than the word for the ceiling of a room.

shell.expression.functions.floor.descrip.en: Largest integer less than or equal to the number.
shell.expression.functions.floor.descrip.context: Suggestion-panel description for the floor function in the formula editor. It rounds downwards, to the nearest whole number that is not above the figure given, and must read clearly differently from the ceiling function directly beside it. Use the established mathematical term rather than the word for the floor of a room.

shell.expression.functions.round.descrip.en: Round to the given number of decimal places.
shell.expression.functions.round.descrip.context: Suggestion-panel description for the round function in the formula editor. Unlike the ceiling and floor functions it rounds to the nearest value, and how many digits are kept after the decimal separator is given as the second argument. 'Decimal places' is the number of digits kept, not the separator character itself.

shell.expression.functions.truncate.desc.en: Integer part of the number (drops the fraction).
shell.expression.functions.truncate.desc.context: Suggestion-panel description for the truncate function in the formula editor. It simply throws the digits after the decimal separator away, without rounding — which is why it differs from the floor function for negative figures. Keep the parenthetical explanation as a parenthesis.

shell.expression.functions.sign.descript.context: Suggestion-panel description for the sign function in the formula editor. 'Sign' here means whether a figure is negative, zero or positive — not a signature and not a notice. Keep the three numerals and their order exactly as written; they are the possible results.

shell.expression.functions.sqrt.descript.context: Suggestion-panel description for the sqrt function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. Use the established mathematical term for the square root in the target language.

shell.expression.functions.pow.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the pow function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. 'Base' is the figure being multiplied by itself and 'exponent' is how many times — the same two words appear in the untranslated call signature beside this text, so use the standard mathematical terms.

shell.expression.functions.exp.descripti.en: e raised to the given power.
shell.expression.functions.exp.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the exp function in the formula editor. The lower-case 'e' is the mathematical constant, so leave the letter as it is rather than expanding or translating it; the sentence says the constant is raised to the power supplied.

shell.expression.functions.log.descripti.en: Logarithm of the number in the given base.
shell.expression.functions.log.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the log function in the formula editor. The point to preserve is that the base is supplied as an argument rather than assumed, so this is not specifically the natural logarithm; use the same word for 'base' as in the description of the power function.

shell.expression.functions.log10.descrip.context: Suggestion-panel description for the log10 function in the formula editor; the name keeps its digits and stays in English. It is the logarithm with the base fixed at ten, in contrast to the neighbouring function that takes the base as an argument. Keep '10' as a numeral.

shell.expression.functions.max.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the max function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. It compares exactly two figures and gives back the greater one — say 'the two', because it takes no more than that, and keep it symmetrical with the wording used for the minimum function.

shell.expression.functions.min.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the min function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. It compares exactly two figures and gives back the lesser one; keep the wording symmetrical with the description of the maximum function so the pair reads as a contrast.

shell.expression.functions.ieeeRemainder.en: IEEE 754 remainder of x divided by y.
shell.expression.functions.ieeeRemainder.context: Suggestion-panel description for the ieeeRemainder function in the formula editor. Leave 'IEEE 754' exactly as it is — the name of the floating-point standard that defines this particular kind of remainder, which is not the same as the ordinary remainder operator. The single letters naming the two arguments also stay as they are, matching the untranslated call signature.

shell.expression.functions.sin.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the sin function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. Keep the parenthetical unit: the angle is measured in radians, not degrees, which is the mistake this note exists to prevent.

shell.expression.functions.cos.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the cos function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. Keep the parenthetical unit: the angle is in radians, not degrees. Match the wording of the sine and tangent notes beside it.

shell.expression.functions.tan.descripti.context: Suggestion-panel description for the tan function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. Keep the parenthetical unit: the angle is in radians, not degrees. Match the wording of the sine and cosine notes beside it.

shell.expression.functions.asin.descript.context: Suggestion-panel description for the asin function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. 'Arc sine' is the standard name for the inverse of the sine, so use the established term in the target language rather than a literal rendering of 'arc'; the result is an angle in radians.

shell.expression.functions.acos.descript.context: Suggestion-panel description for the acos function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. 'Arc cosine' is the standard name for the inverse of the cosine; use the established term in the target language, and the result is an angle in radians.

shell.expression.functions.atan.descript.context: Suggestion-panel description for the atan function in the formula editor, whose abbreviated English name stays as it is. 'Arc tangent' is the standard name for the inverse of the tangent; use the established term in the target language, and the result is an angle in radians.

accounts.title.context: Heading of the screen that lists every account in the system. An account is either a person who signs in or a machine identity that only calls the API, so use a word that covers both.

accounts.singular.context: Heading of the slide-over panel that shows one account's details, used only as a fallback when that account has no display name to show instead. Singular, and it must cover both a person and a machine identity.

accounts.common.yes.context: Read-only answer against the Enabled field in the account detail panel, meaning the account may currently sign in and authenticate. One word, in a narrow two-column layout.

accounts.common.no.context: Read-only answer against the Enabled field in the account detail panel, meaning the account is switched off and cannot sign in or authenticate. One word, in a narrow two-column layout.

accounts.roles.Service.context: Name of the role held by an account that represents a service — the organisational unit that submits data — and which may only submit and read its own data, holding no back-office permissions. Use the same word the product uses for a service everywhere else. It appears in a coloured badge, as a dropdown option and inside sentences, so keep it to one word and make sure it reads naturally mid-sentence.

accounts.roles.Operator.context: Name of the back-office role whose default permissions are read-only: it can view schemas, submissions, dashboards, reports and service status, but change and approve nothing. This is a person who works with the data, not machinery or a switchboard operator. One word; it appears in a badge, in the role dropdown and inside sentences.

accounts.roles.Approver.context: Name of the back-office role whose default permissions are to view submissions and sign them off — approve or reject the data a service submitted for a reporting period. Build it on the same root as the verb used for approving a submission elsewhere in the product. One word; badge, dropdown option and mid-sentence use.

accounts.roles.Admin.context: Name of the role that holds every permission in the system and cannot have any taken away, including managing accounts and API keys, erasing personal data and changing configuration. Keep it as short as the clipped English form allows, since it sits in a badge and a narrow table column.

accounts.kinds.User.context: One of the two account kinds: an interactive account a human signs in with, which can also call the API. Here it means the human-operated variety of account, not the person's role and not the currently signed-in person.

accounts.kinds.Application.context: The other account kind: a machine identity that authenticates only with an API key and can never sign in to the console. 'Application' means a client program, not a form or a request to join.

accounts.kindHints.Application.en: API-only credential (cannot log in to the UI)
accounts.kindHints.Application.context: Guidance under the Kind selector in the account editor while the machine-identity kind is selected: such an account has no password and authenticates only with an API key. 'Log in to the UI' means signing in to this admin console; a key here is a secret credential, never a keyboard key.

accounts.kindHints.User.en: Interactive account (can log in to the UI and call APIs)
accounts.kindHints.User.context: Guidance under the Kind selector in the account editor while the human kind is selected: the person can sign in to this admin console and the same account can also be used to call the API. Keep 'APIs' untranslated.

accounts.status.enabled.context: Labels the checkbox that switches an account on in the editor and the read-only Enabled field in the detail panel; the same word also fills the green status badge in the accounts table. It names a state, so do not use the imperative — this is not a command to enable anything. One word, because badges do not wrap.

accounts.status.disabled.context: Fills the red status badge of an account that has been switched off: it still exists but cannot sign in or authenticate. The opposite of the enabled state and not the same as being deleted. One word; badges do not wrap.

accounts.status.deleted.context: Badge shown in the account detail panel only when the account has been removed but is still retained in storage. Keep it distinct from the disabled state, which is a different condition. One or two words.

accounts.fields.name.context: Heads the first column of the accounts table and labels the account's unique machine-style identifier, which is fixed once the account exists. It refers to that identifier, not to a person's personal name. Very short: the column also carries an avatar and the description beneath.

accounts.fields.label.context: Labels the optional friendly display name shown to people wherever the account appears, as opposed to its fixed identifier. A caption or display name, not a printed sticker and not a classification.

accounts.fields.kind.context: Heads a column of the accounts table and labels the selector that says whether the account is a human, interactive one or a machine identity that only uses an API key. Means type or category; keep it very short for the narrow column.

accounts.fields.role.context: Heads a column of the accounts table and labels the selector for the account's role, the template that seeds its permissions. Use the same word as in the role names themselves; keep it very short.

accounts.fields.status.context: Heads the column that holds the enabled/disabled badge in the accounts table and the active/revoked/expired badge in the API-keys table. One short word.

accounts.fields.email.context: Labels the account's contact address, used for notifications and one-off messages, and also the address of a linked single-sign-on identity. Keep it short: it sits above a narrow input in a two-column form.

accounts.fields.area.context: Labels the optional grouping tag on an account, such as a region or a division; it is informative only and grants no access. An organisational grouping, not a measured surface and not a region of the screen.

accounts.fields.created.context: Heads the column, and labels the field, holding the date an account or an API key was first created. Past participle used as a noun phrase; very short, because the cell holds a formatted date.

accounts.fields.createdBy.context: Heads the column naming the account that created the one on that row. 'by' is agentive — created by that person. Very short; the cell shows a name or a dash.

accounts.fields.modified.context: Labels the field holding when the account was last changed, with the person who changed it appended after the date. A past state, not an instruction to modify anything.

accounts.fields.description.context: Heads the description column of the API-keys table and labels the free-text notes box on an account. Keep it short for the column; the text underneath is truncated when long.

accounts.fields.actions.context: Heads the last, right-aligned column of the accounts table, which contains only the per-row actions menu button. Very short plural noun.

accounts.actions.new.context: Primary toolbar button that opens an empty form for creating an account. 'New' is the act of adding one, not a description of something recently created. Short; the wording is quoted verbatim in the empty-list message, so keep the two in step.

accounts.actions.more.context: Screen-reader name of the toolbar button that opens the overflow menu of list-level actions such as onboarding, refresh, export and import. Describe the action rather than the three-dot icon, and never abbreviate.

accounts.actions.onboardService.context: Menu entry that starts the guided wizard for setting up a new service account — the organisational unit that submits data — optionally issuing its first API key at the same time. 'Onboard' means take into use or set up, never boarding a vehicle.

accounts.actions.onboardOperator.context: Menu entry that starts the guided wizard for setting up a new operator: an interactive back-office account with read-only default permissions. 'Onboard' means set up a new account, never boarding a vehicle.

accounts.actions.refresh.context: Menu entry that reloads the account list from the server. Imperative; nothing is created, changed or sent anywhere.

accounts.actions.exporting.context: Replaces the caption of the spreadsheet-export menu entry while the file is being produced. Present progressive, keep the ellipsis, and fit the same menu row as the resting caption.

accounts.actions.exportCsv.context: Menu entry that downloads the accounts currently listed as a spreadsheet file. Leave the format name CSV untranslated.

accounts.actions.exportJson.context: Menu entry that downloads every account as one machine-readable file, for cloning or seeding another environment; API keys are never included in it. Leave the format name JSON untranslated.

accounts.actions.importing.context: Replaces the caption of the import menu entry while the chosen file is being processed. Present progressive, keep the ellipsis, and fit the same menu row.

accounts.actions.importJson.context: Menu entry that reads an exported accounts file back in, creating accounts that are missing and updating those that already exist. The trailing ellipsis signals that a file picker opens first, so keep it; leave JSON untranslated.

accounts.actions.edit.context: Row-menu entry, and a toolbar button in the detail panel, that opens the account for changing. Imperative verb, very short.

accounts.actions.apiKeys.context: Row-menu entry, and a toolbar button in the detail panel, that opens the dialog listing the account's API keys. A key here is a secret credential the account authenticates with — never a keyboard key and never a database key. Leave API untranslated.

accounts.actions.sendEmail.context: Row-menu entry, and a toolbar button in the detail panel, that opens a form for sending a one-off message to the account's contact address. Imperative; only offered when the account has an address and email is configured.

accounts.actions.viewStatus.context: Row-menu entry, shown only for service accounts, that opens the screen tracking how that service is doing against its reporting obligations. 'Status' here is the submission situation of a service, not the enabled or disabled state of the account.

accounts.actions.exportPersonalData.context: Row-menu entry that downloads a file containing everything the system holds about the person behind this account, so it can be handed over to satisfy a data-subject access request. It only reads: nothing is changed or removed. Secret key values are never part of the file.

accounts.actions.exportData.context: Toolbar button in the account detail panel that downloads everything the system holds about the person behind the account, for a data-subject access request. Deliberately shorter than the equivalent row-menu entry because the toolbar is tight; it only reads data.

accounts.actions.erase.context: Row-menu entry, sub-menu entry and toolbar button that opens the right-to-erasure dialog, where the administrator chooses to anonymise the person's data or delete it outright. Both outcomes are irreversible, so choose a verb at least as forceful as the English and clearly stronger than ordinary deletion; the entry is deliberately styled as dangerous. Leave the acronym GDPR untranslated — the regulation keeps that name in English.

accounts.actions.delete.context: Row-menu entry, and the default action of the split button in the detail panel, that removes the account. Destructive and not undoable, though it is refused while the account still owns submitted data — unlike the erasure action beside it, which overrides that protection. Imperative verb, very short.

accounts.actions.cancel.context: Abandons the account editor, or an in-place edit of an API key description, discarding what was typed. Also used as the hover text and the screen-reader name of the small dismiss button beside that field. Imperative and short.

accounts.actions.save.context: Writes the changes made in the account editor to storage, and captions the confirm button when an API key description is edited in place. 'Save' means store or write, never the sense of saving money or of rescuing something.

accounts.actions.close.context: Dismisses a dialog once there is nothing left to confirm — the API keys list, or a finished erasure. Means dismiss this window; never confuse it with closing a reporting period.

accounts.messages.loadFailed.context: Headline of the red bar shown when the account list could not be fetched from the server; the technical reason is printed underneath it. Short, and past tense.

accounts.messages.actionFailed.context: Headline of the red bar shown when an action taken on an account did not go through; the reason follows underneath. Keep it short and general, because it covers every action on the screen.

accounts.messages.loading.context: Fills a single row of the accounts table while the first page of results is being fetched. One word plus the ellipsis; it reports progress and is neither an error nor an empty result.

accounts.messages.empty.en: No accounts yet — click “New account” to add one.
accounts.messages.empty.context: Replaces the table rows when no account has been created yet, and points at the toolbar button that creates one. The quoted words must match that button's caption exactly in your language. This is not an error.

accounts.validation.emailRequired.context: Stops a brand-new account being saved without a contact address; shown in a red bar at the foot of the editor form, which also jumps back to the General tab. One sentence.

accounts.validation.emailInvalid.context: Shown beneath the email box, and when saving, if what was typed is not a well-formed address. Second person, one sentence, and say what to do rather than only what is wrong.

accounts.aria.viewAccount.context: Screen-reader name of a clickable row in the accounts table; activating the row opens that account's detail panel. Describe the action, not the row itself, and do not abbreviate.

placeholders.name: The account's display name if it has one, otherwise its identifier, e.g. Acme Logistics

accounts.aria.actionsFor.context: Screen-reader name of the three-dot button at the end of a table row, which opens the menu of actions available for that account. Describe the action rather than the icon, and do not abbreviate.

placeholders.name: The account's machine-style identifier, e.g. acme_logistics

accounts.confirmDelete.en:
Delete account "{{target}}"?

This cannot be undone.
accounts.confirmDelete.context: Confirmation asked in a plain browser dialog before an account is removed. Deletion is permanent, so keep the second paragraph as blunt as the English; the blank line between the two sentences is deliberate and must be kept.

placeholders.target: The account's display name if it has one, otherwise its identifier, e.g. Acme Logistics

accounts.import.readError.en: Could not read the accounts file: {{error}}
accounts.import.readError.context: Shown in a red bar when the file chosen for an accounts import cannot be read or is not valid JSON, so nothing was imported. The reason comes from the browser and stays in English; leave it untranslated.

placeholders.error: Raw technical reason the file could not be read or parsed, in English, e.g. Unexpected token < in JSON at position 0

accounts.import.confirm.en:
Import accounts from this file?

Accounts are matched by name: existing ones are updated and new names are created. Accounts not in the file are left untouched.

API keys are NOT included, so any account created by this import starts with no key — generate one for each afterwards.
accounts.import.confirm.context: Confirmation asked in a plain browser dialog before an accounts file is imported, explaining how existing accounts are matched by their identifier and updated, that accounts absent from the file are untouched, and that no API key comes back with the import. Keep the three paragraphs and the emphasis on NOT, because an administrator who misses it will assume the imported accounts can already authenticate.

accounts.import.skipped.context: Optional clause appended to the import summary listing how many entries in the file were rejected and why. 'Skipped' means not imported at all, not postponed.

placeholders.count: Number of entries in the file that were rejected, e.g. 1
placeholders.errors: The rejection reasons, already translated and joined with semicolons, e.g. name already exists

joins.after: The 'updated' count of the import summary sentence, and before that sentence's closing full stop
joins.example: Import complete: 3 created, 2 updated · 1 skipped: name already exists.
joins.note: Keep the leading space and the separator dot, and do not add a full stop — the surrounding sentence supplies it. CJK may drop the leading space only when the first character is full-width.

accounts.import.complete.context: Green bar reporting the outcome of an accounts import: how many accounts were newly created and how many existing ones were updated. Past tense; the optional clause about rejected entries is slotted in before the final full stop.

placeholders.created: Number of accounts the import created, e.g. 3
placeholders.updated: Number of existing accounts the import updated, e.g. 2
placeholders.tail: Either empty, or the assembled clause listing how many entries were skipped and why

accounts.placeholders.email.context: Ghost text in an empty contact-address box, both on an account and on a single-sign-on link. A specimen address: keep it obviously fictional and leave example.com as it is.

accounts.placeholders.area.context: Ghost text in the empty grouping-tag box, offering a specimen tag. Keep the 'e.g.' framing and replace the sample with something equally plausible in the target language.

accounts.editor.newTitle.context: Heading of the slide-over panel while a brand-new account is being filled in. Noun phrase naming what is being created.

accounts.editor.editTitle.context: Heading of the same slide-over panel when an existing account is open for changes. 'Edit' is the action being performed on the account.

accounts.editor.tabs.general.context: First tab of the account editor, holding identity details: identifier, display name, description, contact address, grouping tag, kind, the enabled switch and single-sign-on links. Short noun phrase; users navigate by muscle memory, so keep the wording stable.

accounts.editor.tabs.permissions.context: Second tab of the account editor, holding the role selector and the individual capability checkboxes it seeds. Short noun phrase; keep the same words used for role and for permissions elsewhere.

accounts.editor.emailHint.en: Used for email notifications and ad-hoc messages.
accounts.editor.emailHint.context: Guidance under the contact-address box explaining what the address is used for: automatic notification emails and one-off messages an administrator sends by hand.

accounts.editor.areaHint.context: Guidance under the grouping-tag box: filling it in is optional and it only groups accounts for convenience, granting no access of any kind.

accounts.editor.none.context: Option in the grouping-tag dropdown that clears the tag, and the summary shown while no tag is set. It means no value chosen, not the number zero; keep it to one word.

accounts.editor.roleHint.en: A template that seeds the permissions below — adjust them freely afterwards.
accounts.editor.roleHint.context: Guidance under the role selector: picking a role only pre-fills the capability checkboxes below it, and the administrator may then tick or untick individual capabilities. 'Template' means a starting set that is not binding afterwards.

accounts.scope.title.context: Labels the picker that limits which services an account is allowed to see, and names the same thing as an editor tab, a wizard step and a read-only field. 'Scope' is the boundary of what the account may access, never a telescope or a project's remit. Keep it short, as it has to fit a tab strip.

accounts.scope.hint.en: Which services this account can see. Leave empty for unrestricted access to every service; pick one or more to confine it to just those.
accounts.scope.hint.context: Guidance under the service picker in the account editor: leaving it empty grants access to every service, while choosing one or more confines the account to exactly those. Make the empty-means-everything rule unmistakable, since translators of the label alone have led admins to assume the opposite.

accounts.scope.viewHint.en: Which services this account can see.
accounts.scope.viewHint.context: Guidance beside the read-only list of services an account may see, in the account detail panel. Shorter than the editable version because nothing can be changed here.

accounts.scope.allServices.context: Ghost text and summary shown in the service picker while nothing is selected, meaning the account is not restricted and can see every service. Short enough for a closed dropdown.

accounts.scope.unrestricted.context: Read-only value shown where an account has no service restriction at all, in the detail panel and in the onboarding summary. The parenthesis spells out that this is deliberate breadth rather than a missing setting; keep both parts.

accounts.permissions.title.context: Labels the block of capability checkboxes in the account editor's second tab. Permissions are the individual things an account is allowed to do; keep the same word throughout the product.

accounts.permissions.hint.en: Fine-grained capabilities. The role above is just a starting template — tailor these as needed.
accounts.permissions.hint.context: Guidance above the capability checkboxes: each one grants a single, narrow ability, and the role chosen above only supplies the initial ticks. 'Fine-grained' means individually selectable rather than all-or-nothing.

accounts.permissions.adminNote.en: Administrators always hold every permission; this cannot be reduced.
accounts.permissions.adminNote.context: Explanation shown in place of the capability checkboxes when the role is the all-powerful administrator: it holds every permission and none can be taken away, which is why the checkboxes are locked. State the impossibility plainly.

accounts.permissions.serviceNote.en: Service accounts only submit and view their own data; they hold no back-office permissions.
accounts.permissions.serviceNote.context: Explanation shown in place of the capability checkboxes when the role is a service account: it may only submit and read its own data and holds no back-office permissions at all, which is why the checkboxes are locked. 'Back-office' means the administrative side of the console, as opposed to submitting data.

accounts.onboarding.serviceTitle.context: Heading of the guided, multi-step dialog that sets up a new service — the organisational unit that submits data — as an account, optionally issuing its first API key on the way. 'Onboard' means take into use or set up from scratch.

accounts.onboarding.operatorTitle.context: Heading of the same guided dialog when it is setting up a new operator: an interactive back-office account with read-only default permissions. 'Onboard' means set up from scratch.

accounts.onboarding.createAccount.context: Primary button on the wizard's last step; pressing it actually creates the account and, if asked for, issues its first API key. Imperative and short.

accounts.onboarding.details.title.context: Heading of the wizard's first step, where the account's identifier, display name, contact address and kind are entered. It also appears in the compact step indicator at the top of the dialog, so keep it very short.

accounts.onboarding.details.description.context: One line under the step heading, saying which sort of account this run of the wizard will produce. The role name is inserted verbatim from the role list, so phrase the sentence so it stays correct whichever role appears and take care with articles and agreement.

placeholders.role: The already-translated role name, e.g. Service or Operator

accounts.onboarding.details.nameHint.context: Guidance under the identifier box: the value must be unique across the whole system and is not meant to change afterwards. 'Machine-style' means a plain lowercase token without spaces or accents, as in the example beneath.

accounts.onboarding.details.namePlacehol.context: Ghost text showing the shape of an acceptable identifier: a fictional organisation, lowercase, words joined by an underscore. Keep the 'e.g.' framing and that shape; do not introduce spaces or accented characters.

accounts.onboarding.details.labelPlaceho.context: Ghost text in the display-name box, prompting for the human-readable name shown wherever the account appears. 'Friendly' means easy for people to read, not informal in tone; keep it short enough for a narrow input.

accounts.onboarding.details.emailPlaceho.context: Ghost text in the contact-address box, giving a specimen address for whoever is responsible for the account. Leave example.com untouched and keep the result a valid address with no spaces.

accounts.onboarding.kindHints.Applicatio.en: API-only credential (cannot log in to the UI).
accounts.onboarding.kindHints.Applicatio.context: Guidance under the Kind selector while the machine-identity kind is chosen: the account has no password and can only authenticate with an API key. A key is a secret credential, never a keyboard key.

accounts.onboarding.kindHints.User.en: Interactive account (can log in to the UI and call APIs).
accounts.onboarding.kindHints.User.context: Guidance under the Kind selector while the human kind is chosen: the person can sign in to this console and the same account can also call the API. Keep 'APIs' untranslated.

accounts.onboarding.scope.description.en: Choose which services this {{role}} can see. Leave empty for unrestricted access to every service.
accounts.onboarding.scope.description.context: One line under the heading of the wizard step that limits which services the new account may see, restating that leaving the choice empty grants access to all of them. The role name is inserted verbatim, so keep the sentence grammatical whichever one appears.

placeholders.role: The already-translated role name, e.g. Operator

accounts.onboarding.scope.visibleService.context: Labels the multi-select that lists the services the new account will be allowed to see. 'Visible' describes what the account may look at, not what is currently on screen.

accounts.onboarding.scope.hint.en: Leave empty for unrestricted access to every service; pick one or more to confine this account to just those.
accounts.onboarding.scope.hint.context: Guidance under that multi-select: an empty selection means unrestricted access to every service, while choosing one or more confines the account to exactly those. Make the empty-means-everything rule unmistakable.

accounts.onboarding.key.title.context: Heading of the wizard step that offers to issue the account's first secret credential. Singular, and it also appears in the compact step indicator, so keep it very short; leave API untranslated.

accounts.onboarding.key.description.en: Optionally issue an API key so the account can call the ingest API right away.
accounts.onboarding.key.description.context: One line under that step heading: issuing a key is optional, and doing it here means the account can start sending data immediately. The ingest API is the interface through which data is submitted; leave API untranslated and treat Ingest as the product name.

accounts.onboarding.key.generateNow.context: Labels the checkbox that decides whether a secret credential is issued as part of creating the account. 'Generate' means have the system produce a new secret value; 'now' contrasts with issuing one later.

accounts.onboarding.key.applicationWarni.en: An Application account can only authenticate with an API key. Without one it won't be able to submit data until a key is issued later.
accounts.onboarding.key.applicationWarni.context: Warning bar shown when a machine-identity account is about to be created without a key: since such an account has no other way to prove who it is, it will be unable to send any data until a key is issued. Keep the warning as pointed as the English.

accounts.onboarding.key.descriptionLabel.context: Labels the free-text note attached to the key being issued. Keep the parenthesised '(optional)' so it is clear the box may be left empty.

accounts.onboarding.key.descriptionHint.en: A note on who or why this key is for — handy for temporary or holiday-cover keys.
accounts.onboarding.key.descriptionHint.context: Guidance under that note: it records who the key was issued to or why it exists, which matters most for short-lived keys. 'Holiday cover' means a stand-in for someone who is away — convey the situation rather than the English words.

accounts.onboarding.key.expiryLabel.context: Labels the date after which the key being issued stops working. Keep the parenthesised '(optional)': left empty, the key never expires.

accounts.onboarding.result.created.context: Headline of the wizard's final screen, confirming that the account now exists. Past tense; both the role name and the account's display name are inserted, so keep the sentence natural for any role and remember the quotation marks around the name.

placeholders.role: The already-translated role name, e.g. Service
placeholders.name: The new account's display name, or its identifier when it has none, e.g. Acme Logistics

accounts.onboarding.result.copyKey.en: Copy this API key now — it will not be shown again.
accounts.onboarding.result.copyKey.context: Headline of the warning bar that displays the newly issued secret key value just beneath it. This is the only time the value can ever be seen, so it must be copied before the dialog is dismissed; keep the urgency and the finality of the English.

accounts.onboarding.result.copied.context: Briefly replaces the hover text of the copy button once the key value has been put on the clipboard. Past tense, one word; keep the exclamation only if it reads naturally.

accounts.onboarding.result.copyToClipboa.context: Hover text of the small button beside the newly issued key value, which copies that value to the clipboard. Use the platform's usual wording for the clipboard.

accounts.onboarding.result.copyAria.context: Screen-reader name of that copy button. Describe the action and what is copied — the secret credential — and do not abbreviate.

accounts.onboarding.result.noKey.en: No API key was generated. You can issue one later from the account's API keys dialog.
accounts.onboarding.result.noKey.context: Shown on the final screen in place of a key value when the administrator chose not to issue one, and says that one can still be issued later from the account's API keys dialog. Refer to that dialog with the same words used for the API keys action elsewhere.

accounts.erase.title.context: Heading of the dialog that carries out a right-to-erasure request against one account, naming the person or account concerned. It states the decision being asked for, so use a verb as strong as the English — this is not ordinary deletion of a record.

placeholders.name: The account's display name, or its identifier when it has none, e.g. A. Rossi

accounts.erase.deleted.context: Headline of the green bar shown when erasure finished in delete mode: the account and everything tied to it are gone for good. Past tense and final.

accounts.erase.anonymised.context: Headline of the green bar shown when erasure finished in anonymise mode: the account survives as a meaningless pseudonym with every identifying trace stripped out. Past tense; 'anonymized' means the identity is permanently unrecoverable, not merely hidden from view.

accounts.erase.resultPrefix.context: Introduces the generated stand-in name that replaced the person's identity everywhere in the data. A pseudonym is an artificial substitute identifier; it is machine-generated and must never be translated.

joins.before: The generated pseudonym in monospace, then a separator dot and the tally of affected records
joins.example: Pseudonym erased-8f3a2c · 12 submission(s), 40 sample(s), 3 email(s), 7 audit entr(ies), 2 key(s).
joins.note: Reads as a label immediately followed by its value, with a single space between them and no colon; do not add punctuation of your own.

accounts.erase.resultCounts.en: {{submissions}} submission(s), {{samples}} sample(s), {{emails}} email(s), {{auditEntries}} audit entr(ies), {{keys}} key(s).
accounts.erase.resultCounts.context: Tally of how much data the erasure touched, closing the confirmation line. A submission is one filled-in schema for a reporting period, a sample is one measurement within it, emails are messages held in the outbox, audit entries are records in the accountability trail, and keys are the account's API credentials.

placeholders.submissions: Number of submissions redacted or removed, e.g. 12
placeholders.samples: Number of individual samples redacted or removed, e.g. 40
placeholders.emails: Number of stored outbox messages deleted, e.g. 3
placeholders.auditEntries: Number of audit-log entries rewritten to the pseudonym or deleted, e.g. 7
placeholders.keys: Number of API keys deleted, e.g. 2

joins.after: The pseudonym and a separator dot
joins.example: Pseudonym erased-8f3a2c · 12 submission(s), 40 sample(s), 3 email(s), 7 audit entr(ies), 2 key(s).
joins.note: The English '(s)' and 'entr(ies)' are a shortcut for covering one and many at once; if that trick does not work in your language, choose a form that is correct for any number, since these figures can each be zero or one. Keep the closing full stop.

accounts.erase.warningBefore.en: This satisfies a right-to-erasure request. It is
accounts.erase.warningBefore.context: Opens the warning above the erasure choices: this action exists to satisfy a person's legal request to have their data removed. It runs straight into an emphasised word and then a closing clause.

joins.before: The emphasised word meaning irreversible, then the closing clause of the same sentence
joins.example: This satisfies a right-to-erasure request. It is irreversible and bypasses the usual “account has submitted data” protection.
joins.note: The three pieces are always rendered in this order with one space between them, and only the middle piece is bold. Spread your wording across the pieces so the finished sentence reads naturally, and keep the emphasised piece a single word or short phrase.

accounts.erase.irreversible.context: The bold word in the middle of that warning, carrying the whole weight of the message: once run, the erasure can never be reversed and the data cannot be brought back. Choose the strongest natural equivalent; nothing weaker, such as 'not recommended' or 'hard to undo', is acceptable.

joins.before: The clause beginning 'and bypasses the usual …'
joins.after: The sentence opening 'This satisfies a right-to-erasure request. It is'
joins.example: This satisfies a right-to-erasure request. It is irreversible and bypasses the usual “account has submitted data” protection.
joins.note: Rendered bold, on its own, with a space on each side. Keep it to one word or a very short phrase, and make sure it fits grammatically after the copula in the preceding piece.

accounts.erase.warningAfter.en: and bypasses the usual “account has submitted data” protection.
accounts.erase.warningAfter.context: Closes that warning: erasure also overrides the safeguard that normally refuses to remove an account which owns submitted data. The quoted phrase names that safeguard, so keep it quoted and switch to the quotation marks your language uses.

joins.after: The emphasised word meaning irreversible
joins.example: This satisfies a right-to-erasure request. It is irreversible and bypasses the usual “account has submitted data” protection.
joins.note: A single space is inserted before this piece, and it supplies the sentence's full stop. Do not repeat words from the earlier pieces.

accounts.erase.mode.context: Labels the pair of radio buttons choosing between the two ways of erasing. 'Mode' means method or variant here; keep it to one word.

accounts.erase.anonymiseOption.en: Anonymize — keep numeric/date KPI values for reporting, strip all identity (pseudonymize the account, redact free-text, drop keys & emails).
accounts.erase.anonymiseOption.context: Label of the first radio button, describing the gentler of the two irreversible options: the figures needed for reporting are kept, while every trace of identity is destroyed — the account is renamed to a generated pseudonym, free text is blanked out, and its API keys and stored emails are deleted. KPI values are the numbers and dates being reported; 'redact' means blank out permanently, not hide. Keep the whole enumeration and its parenthesis, and do not imply the identity could be restored.

accounts.erase.deleteOption.en: Delete — permanently remove the account and everything tied to it (submissions, samples, emails, audit trail).
accounts.erase.deleteOption.context: Label of the second radio button: the account and every record attached to it are removed outright, leaving nothing behind — including the reported figures and the accountability trail. 'Permanently' must not be softened, and the list of what goes must stay complete.

accounts.erase.acknowledgement.en: I understand this cannot be undone.
accounts.erase.acknowledgement.context: Labels the checkbox the administrator must tick before the erasure button becomes usable. Keep the first-person voice — it is the administrator accepting responsibility — and keep the statement of finality as plain as the English.

accounts.erase.erasing.context: Replaces the erasure button's caption while the operation is running. Present progressive, keep the ellipsis, and fit the same button as the resting caption.

accounts.erase.deleteEverything.context: Caption of the confirming button while the delete option is selected; pressing it destroys the account and all data tied to it, irreversibly. Imperative and deliberately blunt — the sweeping 'everything' is the point and must survive translation.

accounts.erase.anonymise.context: Caption of the confirming button while the anonymise option is selected; pressing it irreversibly strips the identity while keeping the reportable figures. Imperative, and use the same verb as the option it confirms.

accounts.email.title.context: Heading of the dialog for writing a one-off message to a single account holder. Names the recipient; the message is composed by hand, not generated by the system.

placeholders.name: The account's display name, or its identifier when it has none, e.g. A. Rossi

accounts.email.to.context: First line inside that dialog, showing the address the message will go to. The recipient cannot be changed here, so the line is purely informative; keep the label short, as in an email header.

placeholders.email: The account's contact address, e.g. a.rossi@example.com

accounts.email.subjectRequired.context: Shown in a red bar when the send button is pressed with an empty subject line; nothing is sent. One sentence.

accounts.email.queued.context: Green bar confirming that the message has been accepted into the outbox and will be delivered by the mail sender shortly. Say only that it is waiting to be sent — it has not been delivered yet, and 'queued' must not be translated as 'sent'.

accounts.email.subject.context: Labels the single-line subject of the message being composed. Use the word your language uses in email clients for that header, and keep it short.

accounts.email.message.context: Labels the multi-line body of the message being composed. It refers to the text the administrator types, not to a system notification.

accounts.email.sending.context: Replaces the send button's caption while the message is being handed to the server. Present progressive, keep the ellipsis, and fit the same button as the resting caption.

accounts.email.send.context: Primary button that hands the composed message to the outbox for delivery. Imperative and short.

accounts.sso.title.context: Heads the block that links this account to identities held by an external login provider, and labels the same information in the read-only detail panel. SSO is single sign-on — signing in once with an outside account instead of a password kept here; keep the abbreviation if it is established in your language, otherwise use the accepted local term. Rendered in small capitals in the editor, so keep it short.

accounts.sso.hint.en: Link an identity-provider account so this user can sign in with “Continue with …”. Matched on the provider and the user’s verified email.
accounts.sso.hint.context: Guidance under that heading: adding a link lets this person sign in through an external login provider, and the match is made on the provider plus the address that provider has verified. The quoted words are the caption of the button on the sign-in screen, so use exactly the same wording there; the ellipsis stands for the provider's name.

accounts.sso.provider.context: Labels the dropdown naming which external login service a link uses, such as a corporate directory or a public identity service. Shown only above the first row, acting as a column heading, so keep it to one short word. Provider names themselves are configured by the deployment and are never translated.

accounts.sso.remove.context: Screen-reader name of the small button that deletes one single-sign-on link row, after which that external identity can no longer be used to sign in. Describe the action rather than the bin icon, and do not abbreviate.

accounts.sso.add.context: Button that appends an empty row for one more external identity link. Imperative and short; it only adds the row, nothing is saved until the account is saved.

accounts.audit.title.context: Small heading in capitals over the account's creation and last-change record. 'Audit' is the accountability trail of who did what and when, not a financial inspection; keep it to one word.

accounts.audit.by.context: Attributes a change to the account that made it, appended straight after a rendered date and time. 'by' is agentive — performed by that person.

placeholders.name: Display name of the account that performed the action, e.g. A. Rossi

joins.after: A formatted date and time in the Created or Modified field of the account detail panel
joins.note: Keep the leading space and the separator dot; CJK may drop the space only when the first character is full-width. Nothing follows it, so add no full stop.

accounts.keys.title.context: Heading of the dialog listing one account's API keys, where keys are issued, revoked and deleted. A key here is a secret credential the account authenticates with — never a keyboard key or a database key. Leave API untranslated.

placeholders.name: The account's display name, or its identifier when it has none, e.g. Acme Logistics

accounts.keys.copyNow.en: Copy this key now — it will not be shown again.
accounts.keys.copyNow.context: Headline of the warning bar that shows a freshly issued secret key value just below it. The value is displayed this once and can never be recovered afterwards, so it must be copied before the dialog is closed; keep the warning as emphatic as the English.

accounts.keys.keyId.context: Heads the column holding a key's short public identifier, which is how one key is told apart from another in the list and in the logs. It is not the secret value and is safe to show; the identifiers themselves are never translated. Very short — the column is narrow.

accounts.keys.expires.context: Heads the column holding the date on which a key stops being accepted. Present tense as a heading, not a past event; very short, because the cell holds a date.

accounts.keys.never.context: Fills the expiry cell of a key that was issued without an end date, so it keeps working until it is revoked. One word, in a column that does not wrap.

accounts.keys.revoke.context: Small button in a key's row that withdraws that key immediately: anything using it stops working at once, and the key stays in the list marked as withdrawn. Irreversible — a revoked key can never be reinstated, only replaced — so use a verb that carries that finality. Short enough for a compact button.

accounts.keys.delete.context: Hover text of the small bin button in a key's row, which removes the key from the list altogether rather than merely withdrawing it. Short, and keep 'key' in the sense of a secret credential.

accounts.keys.deleteAria.context: Screen-reader name of that bin button, naming which key it would remove. Describe the action, not the icon, and do not abbreviate.

placeholders.keyId: The key's short public identifier, shown verbatim and never translated, e.g. ak_7f3c91

accounts.keys.saveDescription.context: Screen-reader name of the tick button that commits an in-place edit of a key's note. 'Save' means store the changed text; describe the action, not the icon.

accounts.keys.editDescription.context: Hover text of the pencil button in a key's row, which turns that key's note into an editable box; the same wording is announced to screen readers, so it must work as a spoken action and never be abbreviated.

accounts.keys.nextDescription.context: Labels the note that will be attached to the key issued by the button at the foot of the dialog — it does not change any existing key. 'Next' means the one about to be created; keep the parenthesised '(optional)'.

accounts.keys.descriptionHint.en: A note on who or why this key is for — handy for temporary or holiday-cover keys, especially with an expiry.
accounts.keys.descriptionHint.context: Guidance under that note: it records who the key was issued to or why it exists, which matters most for short-lived keys given an expiry date. 'Holiday cover' means standing in for someone who is away — convey the situation rather than the English words.

accounts.keys.descriptionPlaceholderShor.context: Ghost text of the small note box that appears inside a table cell while a key's note is edited in place. It must be noticeably shorter than the version used in the form below, since the cell is narrow; keep the 'e.g.' framing and replace the personal name with one natural in your language.

accounts.keys.descriptionPlaceholder.context: Ghost text of the note box for the key about to be issued, both in the keys dialog and in the onboarding wizard. The parenthesis shows that naming the person's role is useful; keep the 'e.g.' framing and use a personal name that reads naturally in your language.

accounts.keys.nextExpiry.context: Labels the end date that will be given to the key issued by the button at the foot of the dialog; it does not change any existing key. Keep the parenthesised '(optional)'.

accounts.keys.expiryHint.en: Leave blank for a key that never expires. Maximum two years from today.
accounts.keys.expiryHint.context: Guidance under that date box: an empty value means the key stays valid indefinitely, and the server refuses any date more than two years ahead. State both facts; the two-year limit is enforced, not advisory.

accounts.keys.generate.context: Primary button that issues one more secret credential for the account, using the note and expiry entered above. It adds a key: keys already in the list keep working until they are revoked, so do not imply that the old one is replaced. Imperative.

accounts.keys.confirmDeleteRevoked.en:
Permanently delete API key {{keyId}}?

This removes the revoked key from the list for good.

This cannot be undone.
accounts.keys.confirmDeleteRevoked.context: Confirmation asked in a plain browser dialog before an already-withdrawn key is removed from the list. Nothing stops working — the key was dead already — but the record of it disappears for good; keep the closing sentence about it being final, and keep the blank lines between the paragraphs.

placeholders.keyId: The key's short public identifier, shown verbatim and never translated, e.g. ak_7f3c91

accounts.keys.confirmDeleteActive.en:
Permanently delete API key {{keyId}}?

The key is still active — deleting it stops it working immediately, just like revoking, but also removes it from the list.

This cannot be undone.
accounts.keys.confirmDeleteActive.context: Confirmation asked in a plain browser dialog before a key that is still in use is removed. Say plainly that whatever uses this key stops working the moment it is deleted, exactly as if it had been withdrawn, and that the record goes too; the consequence is immediate and cannot be undone. Keep the blank lines between the paragraphs.

placeholders.keyId: The key's short public identifier, shown verbatim and never translated, e.g. ak_7f3c91

accounts.keys.status.revoked.context: Red badge on a key that has been deliberately withdrawn and will never be accepted again. One word; badges do not wrap. Keep it distinct from a key that merely reached its end date.

accounts.keys.status.expired.context: Red badge on a key that has passed the end date it was given, so it is no longer accepted even though nobody withdrew it. One word; badges do not wrap.

accounts.keys.status.active.context: Green badge on a key that is currently accepted for authentication. One word, and 'active' here means in force, not busy or in use at this moment.

tools.title.context: Heading of the screen holding the console's maintenance utilities — today the backup, restore and account-transfer tools. Plural noun phrase; these are operational instruments, not configuration settings.

tools.loading.context: Caption beside the spinner shown while the signed-in account's permissions are being fetched, before the screen can be drawn. One word plus the ellipsis.

tools.noPermission.en: You don't have permission to use these tools.
tools.noPermission.context: Red bar shown in place of the whole screen when the signed-in account lacks the permission needed to take backups. Second person, one sentence; it states what this account is not allowed to do rather than reporting a failure.

tools.navigationGroup.context: Heading in small capitals over the group of entries in this screen's left-hand list; every tool on the screen sits beneath it. Very short, and it names the pair of opposite operations — taking a copy of the data and putting one back.

tools.preparing.context: Replaces a download button's caption while the server assembles the file. Present progressive, keep the ellipsis, and fit the same button as the resting caption.

tools.restoring.context: Replaces the restore button's caption while the uploaded file is being written back over the current data. Present progressive, keep the ellipsis, and fit the same button as the resting caption.

tools.importing.context: Replaces the import button's caption while the chosen accounts file is being processed. Present progressive, keep the ellipsis, and fit the same button as the resting caption.

tools.restoreFromFile.context: Button that picks a backup file and, after a confirmation, writes its contents over everything currently stored. Destructive: keep 'restore' clearly distinct from exporting or importing, and keep the trailing ellipsis, which signals that a file picker opens first.

tools.importFromFile.context: Button that picks an accounts file and merges it into the existing accounts, creating those that are missing and updating those that are present. Unlike a restore, nothing is wiped; keep the trailing ellipsis, which signals that a file picker opens first.

tools.restoreComplete.context: Green bar shown when a restore has finished; a list of how many records were written per category follows underneath. Past tense and short, since it is only the lead-in to that list.

tools.dataBackup.title.context: Names the tool that copies the whole stored data set to a file and puts it back again; used both as the entry in this screen's left-hand list and as the heading of its card. Short noun phrase, because the list is narrow.

tools.dataBackup.description.en: Export the entire registry (accounts, keys, schemas, submissions, reports, audit log) to a single JSON file, or restore it from one.
tools.dataBackup.description.context: Explains what that tool does: it writes everything the system holds — accounts, API keys, schemas, submissions, reports and the audit log — into one machine-readable file, and can read such a file back. Keep the list of contents intact and use the product's established word for each item; leave JSON untranslated.

tools.dataBackup.readError.en: Could not read the backup file: {{error}}
tools.dataBackup.readError.context: Shown in a red bar when the chosen backup file cannot be read or is not valid JSON, so nothing was restored. The reason comes from the browser in English and stays as it is.

placeholders.error: Raw technical reason the file could not be read or parsed, in English, e.g. Unexpected end of JSON input

tools.dataBackup.confirmRestore.en:
Restore from this backup?

This REPLACES all current data (accounts, keys, schemas, submissions, reports, audit log) with the contents of the file. It cannot be undone. Make sure you have a current backup first.
tools.dataBackup.confirmRestore.context: Confirmation asked in a plain browser dialog before a backup file overwrites the live data. This is the most destructive action in the console: everything currently stored is thrown away and replaced, with no way back, which is why the administrator is told to take a fresh backup first. The capitals on REPLACES carry that emphasis — reproduce it however your language emphasises a word — and keep the blank line between the paragraphs.

tools.dataBackup.warningBeforeSmall.en: This is a convenience tool for
tools.dataBackup.warningBeforeSmall.context: Opens the standing warning on the data-backup card: this tool is a convenience, not a substitute for proper backups. It runs straight into an emphasised word.

joins.before: The emphasised word meaning small, then the rest of the paragraph
joins.example: This is a convenience tool for small deployments and moving data between environments — not the primary backup mechanism. For real backups, take a database-level snapshot (mongodump or your hosting provider's backup). A restore replaces all current data and is not transactional.
joins.note: The paragraph is assembled from several pieces in a fixed order with one space between them, and only some are bold. Distribute your wording so the finished paragraph reads naturally, and keep each emphasised piece as short as it is in English.

tools.dataBackup.small.context: The emphasised word qualifying which deployments this tool suits: ones holding modest amounts of data. It attaches to the word for deployments that follows it, so use whatever form agrees with that noun.

joins.after: The opening words 'This is a convenience tool for'
joins.before: The word for deployments and the rest of the paragraph
joins.example: This is a convenience tool for small deployments and moving data between environments — not the primary backup mechanism.
joins.note: Rendered bold with a space on each side; keep it to one word.

tools.dataBackup.warningBeforeNot.en: deployments and moving data between environments —
tools.dataBackup.warningBeforeNot.context: Continues the warning: the tool also suits carrying data from one environment to another, such as from a test system to a live one. The dash sets up the contrast with the emphasised phrase that follows.

joins.after: The emphasised word meaning small
joins.before: The emphasised phrase denying that this is the main backup mechanism
joins.example: This is a convenience tool for small deployments and moving data between environments — not the primary backup mechanism.
joins.note: Begins with the noun that the preceding bold adjective qualifies, and ends with the dash. Keep the dash, using the punctuation your language prefers for such an aside.

tools.dataBackup.notPrimary.context: The emphasised denial at the heart of the warning: nobody should rely on this file as their real backup. 'Primary' means the one relied upon, and 'mechanism' the arrangement for taking backups; keep the negation forceful.

joins.after: The dash closing 'deployments and moving data between environments —'
joins.example: This is a convenience tool for small deployments and moving data between environments — not the primary backup mechanism. For real backups, take a database-level snapshot (mongodump …
joins.note: Rendered bold and it supplies its own full stop; a space is inserted before the sentence that follows.

tools.dataBackup.warningBeforeCommand.en: For real backups, take a database-level snapshot (
tools.dataBackup.warningBeforeCommand.context: Introduces the advice on what a real backup looks like: a copy taken at the database level rather than through this screen. It breaks off at an opening bracket, which is immediately followed by the name of a database utility.

joins.before: The command name mongodump, in monospace, with no space in between
joins.example: For real backups, take a database-level snapshot (mongodump or your hosting provider's backup).
joins.note: Keep the opening bracket at the very end and add no space after it; the closing bracket is supplied by the following piece. Never translate the command name.

tools.dataBackup.warningBeforeReplace.en: or your hosting provider's backup). A restore
tools.dataBackup.warningBeforeReplace.context: Closes that bracket by naming the alternative — the backup facility offered by whoever hosts the deployment — and starts the final sentence about what a restore does. 'Hosting provider' is the company running the servers.

joins.after: The command name mongodump, in monospace, separated by one space
joins.before: The emphasised phrase about replacing all current data
joins.example: For real backups, take a database-level snapshot (mongodump or your hosting provider's backup). A restore replaces all current data and is not transactional.
joins.note: Keep the closing bracket and the full stop that end the first sentence, and leave the last clause hanging so the bold phrase can follow it.

tools.dataBackup.replacesAll.context: The emphasised phrase spelling out the consequence of a restore: every record now in the system is discarded in favour of the file's contents. This is the destructive core of the warning and must not be softened into 'updates' or 'merges'.

joins.after: The words 'A restore'
joins.before: The closing clause 'and is not transactional.'
joins.example: A restore replaces all current data and is not transactional.
joins.note: Rendered bold with a space on each side, and it must agree with the subject supplied by the preceding piece.

tools.dataBackup.warningAfterReplace.context: Ends the warning: a restore is not all-or-nothing, so if it fails part-way the data is left half-replaced. 'Transactional' is the database sense — either everything is applied or nothing is; keep the technical term administrators will recognise.

joins.after: The emphasised phrase about replacing all current data
joins.example: A restore replaces all current data and is not transactional.
joins.note: A space is inserted before it and it supplies the final full stop; nothing follows.

tools.dataBackup.download.context: Primary button that produces the data-backup file and saves it to the administrator's machine. Imperative and short; it only reads, nothing is changed.

tools.configBackup.title.context: Names the tool that copies the deployment's configuration to a file and puts it back again; used both as the entry in this screen's left-hand list and as the heading of its card. Configuration here means the settings, not the collected data.

tools.configBackup.description.en: Export all configuration (approval policy & rules, email & notification settings and templates, webhooks, integrations and the Teams connection) to a single JSON file, or restore it from one — to copy configuration between environments or recover after a disaster.
tools.configBackup.description.context: Explains what that tool covers: the approval policy and its rules, email and notification settings and templates, webhooks, integrations and the Microsoft Teams connection — useful for copying settings to another environment or rebuilding after a disaster. Keep the list intact, keep Teams as the product name, and leave JSON untranslated.

tools.configBackup.readError.en: Could not read the configuration file: {{error}}
tools.configBackup.readError.context: Shown in a red bar when the chosen configuration file cannot be read or is not valid JSON, so nothing was restored. The reason comes from the browser in English and stays as it is.

placeholders.error: Raw technical reason the file could not be read or parsed, in English, e.g. Unexpected token } in JSON at position 42

tools.configBackup.confirmRestore.en:
Restore from this configuration backup?

This REPLACES all current configuration (approval policy & rules, email & notification settings and templates, webhooks, integrations and the Teams connection) with the contents of the file. It cannot be undone.

Encrypted secrets (SMTP password, webhook secrets, Teams bot secret) only work if this server uses the same ApiKey:Pepper as the one that produced the file; otherwise re-enter them afterwards. A stored secret is kept when the file omits it.
tools.configBackup.confirmRestore.context: Confirmation asked in a plain browser dialog before a configuration file overwrites the live settings: everything listed is discarded in favour of the file, with no way back. The second half warns that encrypted secrets travel as ciphertext and can only be decrypted by a server configured with the same pepper value, so on any other deployment they must be typed in again; a secret already stored is left alone when the file has none. Keep the capitals on REPLACES as emphasis, keep the blank lines, and never translate the setting name ApiKey:Pepper or the product name Teams.

tools.configBackup.warningBeforeReplace.context: Single word opening the standing warning on the configuration-backup card, naming the act of putting a saved configuration back. Use a form that can take the emphasised phrase that follows as its object — a gerund or verbal noun.

joins.before: The emphasised phrase about replacing all current configuration
joins.example: Restoring replaces all current configuration and is not transactional. Encrypted secrets are included as ciphertext and only decrypt on a server using the same ApiKey:Pepper; on a different deployment, re-enter them after the restore.
joins.note: One space is inserted after it; it is the subject of the sentence the next piece completes.

tools.configBackup.replacesAll.context: The emphasised phrase spelling out the consequence: every current setting is discarded in favour of the file's contents. Do not weaken it into merging or updating; this is destructive and cannot be undone.

joins.after: The word for restoring
joins.before: The clause beginning 'and is not transactional.'
joins.example: Restoring replaces all current configuration and is not transactional.
joins.note: Rendered bold with a space on each side, and it must agree with the subject supplied by the preceding piece.

tools.configBackup.warningBeforePepper.en: and is not transactional. Encrypted secrets are included as ciphertext and only decrypt on a server using the same
tools.configBackup.warningBeforePepper.context: Continues the warning: a restore is not all-or-nothing, and the encrypted secrets inside the file can only be read back by a server configured with the identical pepper value. 'Ciphertext' is data in encrypted form; a pepper is a server-wide secret mixed into encryption, and the setting that holds it is named next.

joins.after: The emphasised phrase about replacing all current configuration
joins.before: The setting name ApiKey:Pepper in monospace, separated by one space
joins.example: Restoring replaces all current configuration and is not transactional. Encrypted secrets are included as ciphertext and only decrypt on a server using the same ApiKey:Pepper; on a different deployment, re-enter them after the restore.
joins.note: Must end so that the setting name follows naturally, and the setting name itself is never translated.

tools.configBackup.warningAfterPepper.en: ; on a different deployment, re-enter them after the restore. A stored secret is preserved when the file omits it.
tools.configBackup.warningAfterPepper.context: Ends the warning: on any server with a different pepper the secrets are unreadable and must be typed in again after restoring, while a secret already held is kept if the file does not carry one. 'Re-enter' means type the value in afresh.

joins.after: The setting name ApiKey:Pepper in monospace, with no space in between
joins.example: … only decrypt on a server using the same ApiKey:Pepper; on a different deployment, re-enter them after the restore. A stored secret is preserved when the file omits it.
joins.note: It must begin with the punctuation that follows the setting name, with no leading space, since it is glued directly to it. It supplies the final full stop.

tools.configBackup.download.context: Primary button that produces the configuration file and saves it to the administrator's machine. Imperative and short; it only reads, nothing is changed.

tools.accountsBackup.title.context: Names the tool that copies every account to a file and reads such a file back; used both as the entry in this screen's left-hand list and as the heading of its card. Use exactly the same word as the Accounts screen itself.

tools.accountsBackup.description.en: Export every account (name, label, role, permissions, SSO links, enabled state) to a single JSON file, or import one to create and update accounts — handy for cloning or seeding an environment.
tools.accountsBackup.description.context: Explains what that tool covers: each account's identifier, display name, role, permissions, single-sign-on links and whether it is switched on, written to one file that can be read back to create and update accounts — handy for cloning or seeding an environment. Keep the list intact and use the product's established word for each item; leave JSON untranslated.

tools.accountsBackup.readError.en: Could not read the accounts file: {{error}}
tools.accountsBackup.readError.context: Shown in a red bar when the chosen accounts file cannot be read or is not valid JSON, so nothing was imported. The reason comes from the browser in English and stays as it is.
